The stdio server exposes one MCP tool for each of these CLI workflows,
plus sandboxed recipe and easyblock tools:

- `eb_package_inspect`, `eb_package_plan`, `eb_package_bump`;
- `eb_recipe_read`, `eb_recipe_list`, `eb_recipe_edit`, `eb_recipe_write`,
  `eb_recipe_grep`, `eb_recipe_apply_suggestion`, `eb_recipe_diff`,
  `eb_dep_versions`;
- `eb_recipe_easyblock`, `eb_recipe_templates`, `eb_recipe_hierarchy`;
- `eb_recipe_check`, `eb_recipe_lint`, `eb_recipe_format`;
- `eb_module_lint`, `eb_easyblock_dry_run`, `eb_build_log`, `eb_build_test`
  (easyblocks; `eb_build_test` only with `EB_STACK_ALLOW_BUILD=1`);
- `eb_stack_solve`, `eb_stack_sbom`, `eb_stack_order`,
  `eb_stack_easystack`, `eb_stack_sections`, `eb_stack_from_commit`;
- `eb_target_list`, `eb_target_doctor`;
- `eb_campaign_run`, `eb_campaign_status`;
- `eb_campaign_finding_claim`, `eb_campaign_finding_resolve`;
- `eb_pr_overlap` (the same writer as `pr-overlap`, including
  `--kind easyconfigs`, a merge order, and `--impact`),
  `eb_rebuild_set`, `eb_component_reach`, `eb_easyblock_reach`;
- `eb_repro_summary`.

`eb_recipe_read`, `eb_recipe_list`, `eb_recipe_edit`, `eb_recipe_write`, and
`eb_recipe_grep` resolve every path inside that root. A `..` component, an
absolute path outside the root, or a symlink whose target leaves the root is
rejected and the file is not opened. `eb_recipe_edit` replaces an exact
string. If `old` matches more than once, the file is left unchanged unless
`replace_all` is true. `eb_recipe_write` does not create parent directories.
`eb_recipe_grep` searches for a literal `pattern` (a regular expression when
`regex` is true) under `path` (default the root), skips `.git`, does not
follow symlinks, and returns at most `max_matches` (default and limit 200)
matches. `eb_recipe_check` requires `easyconfigs` (`minItems` 1). An empty
list returns `argument easyconfigs requires at least one path`. A `.eb` file
there means the `easyconfigs` directory it sits in; any other file is an
error that asks for a robot directory. A recipe that is not valid Python is
refused. It also takes `recipe`, `require_configopts`, `easyblocks`,
`metadata_only`, `verify_sources`, `seeded_from`, `seeded_source_url`,
`seeded_git`, `source_tree`, and `strict`, and returns maintainer
acceptability, easyblock resolution, strict skips, and source classes.
`eb_recipe_lint` takes a `recipes` path array and returns `results` plus
`check_contrib`, using the same findings and maintainer-acceptability as
`recipe lint`. `eb_recipe_format` takes `recipe`, `out`, and `dry_run`, and a
dry run does not write.

`eb_recipe_easyblock` takes `name` and `charmap`. `charmap` true prints the
encoding table; a name prints the derived class. `eb_recipe_templates`
takes `name`, `version`, and `export`. `export` true prints the constant
table and the derived-key rules. `eb_recipe_hierarchy` takes `export`.
The plain call prints the fixture generations. `export` true adds the
synthetic GCC-family rule, the same split as `recipe hierarchy --export`.
`eb_stack_order` requires `easyconfigs` and `root`, and takes `out`,
`oldest`, `easystack_out`, `hashes_out`, and `filter_deps`.
`filter_deps` drops the same dependencies `--filter-deps` drops.
`eb_stack_easystack` requires `lock` and takes `out` and `option`, each
option a `<file.eb>:<option>=<value>` string. `eb_stack_sections` requires
`list`, `from`, and `out`, and takes `unfiled`. `eb_stack_from_commit`
requires `easystack` and takes `easyconfigs_repo`, `easyblocks_repo`,
`easybuild_version`, and `json`. It returns the same report as
`stack from-commit`. `eb_repro_summary`
requires `scores` and takes `ratchet` and `json`. Each of these tools
calls the same runner as the command of that name, and the text it
returns is that command's stdout.

The recipe tools run the same checks as the CLI. MCP results include the same
artifacts, claims, findings, and next actions as the CLI. There is no separate
compatibility command surface.

`eb_package_plan` accepts the CLI's repeated source-checksum input as a
`source_checksums` string array, and the catalog / source-root inputs as
`package_catalogs`, `package_sources`, `easybuild_sources`, `conda_sources`,
`spack_sources`, and `cargo_sources` arrays. `emit_easyblock` asks for an
easyblock skeleton in the bundle and does not combine with package-closure
planning. `eb_package_plan` also takes `package_index`, a CRAN
`PACKAGES` file or a `name==version` list, the same input as
`--package-index`. `eb_package_bump` optionals include `version`,
`source_checksum`, `dependencies` (object map), `hierarchy_fixture`,
`stack_policy`, `package_configs`, `emit_easyblock`, `fetch_checksums`,
and `strict_patches`.
`strict_patches` fails the bump when a patch's fate cannot be decided,
as `--strict-patches` does. `fetch_checksums` downloads the new source
and writes its SHA-256, as `--fetch-checksums` does.
`eb_package_inspect`, `eb_package_plan`, and `eb_package_bump` require
`toolchain` as `name/version` or `system`. The schema says so with
`anyOf`, because the retired split fields still satisfy the tools. As on
the command line, `eb_package_inspect` and `eb_package_plan` accept a
lone `toolchain_version` and use `foss`. `eb_package_bump` does not.
`eb_stack_solve` reads the policy file as `stack_policy`.
`eb_recipe_lint` takes a `recipes` path array, or a single `recipe` path, and returns
reviewer-style findings plus `check_contrib`. `eb_campaign_finding_resolve`
takes `changes` as an optional path array. `eb_recipe_check`'s
`easyconfigs` array has `minItems` 1. `eb_recipe_read`, `eb_recipe_list`,
`eb_recipe_edit`, and `eb_recipe_write` edit files only inside the workspace
root.

# Model Context Protocol server

`eb-stack mcp` serves the version-one commands on stdin and stdout.
One JSON-RPC object occupies one line. `--workspace` sets the root for
the recipe file tools and exports `EB_STACK_WORKSPACE` for that process.
When the flag is omitted, an existing `EB_STACK_WORKSPACE` is kept.
Otherwise the server uses its current directory. `eb-stack mcp --help`
prints those flags and exits 0.

The registry manifest is `server.json` at the repository root. The file
uses the 2025-12-11 server schema
([server.schema.json](https://static.modelcontextprotocol.io/schemas/2025-12-11/server.schema.json)).
The server name is `io.github.HaoZeke/eb-stack`. The package is the cargo
crate `eb_stack` at the version in `Cargo.toml`, from `https://crates.io`,
with transport `stdio`. One positional argument is `mcp`. `--workspace`
is an optional named argument. Cargo installs the binary named
`eb-stack`. The manifest has no runtime hint: `cargo install` runs once,
and the client then runs that binary by name.

# Build the binary

Rust 1.88 or newer builds this tree. The binary that the snippets below
call is `eb-stack`.

```bash
cargo build --locked --release
install -Dm755 target/release/eb-stack ~/.local/bin/eb-stack
eb-stack mcp --help
```

# Claude Desktop

Claude Desktop reads `claude_desktop_config.json`. On macOS that file is
`~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`. On
Windows it is `%APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json`. The
top-level key is `mcpServers`. Restart Claude Desktop after saving the
file. This client does not expand `${workspaceFolder}`. Put an absolute
path in `--workspace`.

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "eb-stack": {
      "command": "eb-stack",
      "args": ["mcp", "--workspace", "/absolute/path/to/the/clone"]
    }
  }
}
```

# Visual Studio Code and Copilot

A portable file uses a top-level `mcpServers` object. The Visual Studio
Code file uses a top-level `servers` object. Copying one file onto the
other without changing that key drops the server.

The Visual Studio Code file is `.vscode/mcp.json` in the workspace, or
`mcp.json` in the user profile. `${workspaceFolder}` expands in that
file. `type` is `stdio`.

```json
{
  "servers": {
    "eb-stack": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "eb-stack",
      "args": ["mcp", "--workspace", "${workspaceFolder}"]
    }
  }
}
```

A workspace-root `.mcp.json` uses `mcpServers`. The Copilot user file
does too. That user file is `$COPILOT_HOME/mcp-config.json`, or
``/.copilot/mcp-config.json` when `COPILOT_HOME~ is unset. A portable
file does not expand Visual Studio Code input variables. Pass an
absolute path there.

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "eb-stack": {
      "command": "eb-stack",
      "args": ["mcp", "--workspace", "/absolute/path/to/the/clone"]
    }
  }
}
```

# Tools

`tools/list` returns the workflows of `package`, `recipe`, `stack`,
`target`, `campaign`, and `repro`, plus `pr-overlap`, `rebuild-set`,
`component-reach`, and `easyblock-reach`. `eb_build_test` runs only
when `EB_STACK_ALLOW_BUILD=1`.

# Package bundle reference

`package inspect`, `package plan`, and `package bump` write a version-one
package bundle. The bundle is the hand-off between parsing, Resolvo, EasyBuild
authoring, and empirical build evaluation.

# Bundle layout

```text
BUNDLE/
  package.plan.json
  package.sbom.cdx.json
  closure.plan.json
  closure.sbom.cdx.json
  build-order.json
  locks/<profile>.lock.json
  easyconfigs/<letter>/<name>/<recipe>.eb
  easyconfigs/<letter>/<name>/<patch files>
  easyblocks/<letter>/<module>.py
  packages/<name>-<version>-<toolchain>/
```

`package inspect` writes only the plan and planned Software Bill of Materials (SBOM). `package plan` and
`package bump` also write one lock and one EasyBuild recipe for every requested
profile. A campaign requires at least one lock and recipe.

`package plan` writes `closure.plan.json`, `closure.sbom.cdx.json`, and
`build-order.json` whenever `--easyconfigs` is passed, because that tree is a
discovery root. `--package-catalog` and `--package-sources` add further
providers. Companions land under `packages/<name>-<version>-<toolchain>/`,
beside one shared `easyconfigs/` overlay. Companion providers may be
`foreign` or `easybuild-bump`; bump companions keep `origin = easy-build`
and use the annual-bump emitter. `--emit-easyblock` does not combine with
this writer.

# Canonical package plan

`package.plan.json` is the build manifest. Its `schema_version` is `1` and
unknown fields are rejected by the Rust model.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `origin` | `conda-forge`, `spack`, `easy-build`, `pypi`, `cran`, `cargo`, `luarocks`, or `raku` |
| `package` | Normalized name, version, homepage, description, and license |
| `sources` | URLs, filenames, SHA-256 values, version control system (VCS) identities, staging directories, and provenance |
| `dependencies` | Names, constraints, optional explicit EasyBuild toolchains, roles, structured conditions, virtual capabilities, and provenance |
| `rules` | Preserved conflicts and requirements |
| `build` | Toolchain, easyblock, build systems, configuration options, checksummed patches, typed easyconfig parameters, and module class |
| `profiles` | Independently installable product configurations |
| `outputs` | Requested profile and stack-policy pairs |
| `residuals` | Explicit parser, normalization, resolution, emission, build, or verification work |

Source and dependency provenance records the input span, extractor, original
text, and one of `exact`, `derived`, or `ambiguous`. The static foreign
adapters preserve facts they can prove and put dynamic or ambiguous logic in
`residuals` instead of inventing EasyBuild metadata.

Written provenance paths are source identities rather than checkout locations:
`conda-forge/recipe.yaml`, `spack/package.py`, or the corresponding EasyBuild
recipe name. Line and column spans still address the named input. Absolute
checkout paths are used while reading local inputs but are not serialized into
the bundle, so identical inputs produce identical manifests on different hosts.

An EasyBuild-origin dependency carries `toolchain` when its tuple names an
explicit dependency toolchain. Annual bump planning maps that toolchain family
onto the target generation and requires Resolvo to select a matching artifact.
An implicit tuple omits `toolchain` and may select the minimum non-SYSTEM
member of the target hierarchy. SYSTEM is eligible only when the source tuple
or parent recipe selects it explicitly.

Parser notes are diagnostics. Canonical planning never
searches note text for words such as `dynamic` or `residual`. A successfully
materialized `url_for_version`, for example, may remain visible as a note but
does not create residual work. Anything that needs mechanical repair or
authoring judgment is represented by a typed residual with `category`,
`severity`, `summary`, optional `evidence`, and optional source `provenance`.
Conda `build.number` and compiler, standard-library, or `cross-python` template
requirements are also notes because the EasyBuild toolchain represents those
concerns. An unresolved template in an ordinary package identity remains a
`template-evaluation` residual.

Residual severity has three values:

- `mechanical`: deterministic formatting or metadata work;
- `judgment`: package-authoring or target evidence is required;
- `blocking`: the next pipeline stage cannot make a valid claim.

```json
{
  "id": "foreign:imperative-patch:0",
  "stage": "parse",
  "category": "imperative-patch",
  "severity": "judgment",
  "summary": "imperative patch method requires EasyBuild translation",
  "provenance": {
    "span": {"path": "package.py", "start_line": 42}
  }
}
```

The build manifest stores patches as artifacts:

```json
{
  "filename": "Orbit-2.0-portability.patch",
  "sha256": "4f43b42fdcf84d0cf634d993dd944f252c8243dc612a919fe2825d56f937c8eb",
  "source": "patches/Orbit-2.0-portability.patch"
}
```

Relative patch sources resolve against the package-policy TOML. Planning
verifies the declared SHA-256 before copying each patch beside every emitted
recipe. The manifest retains the portable source path; machine-local resolved
paths do not enter the bundle.

Spack `patch()` directives retain their checksum, exact remote URL, source
provenance, and structured `when` condition. Package-version predicates are
specialized against the selected version; profile predicates remain attached
until variant materialization. A remote artifact has a conventional
`filename`, a `url`, a `sha256`, and a `condition`:

```json
{
  "filename": "26aac9a2adb9a688ab8fe2a9664450de97557cf9.patch",
  "sha256": "54484b722df264dae3fd0c1094883b17431617e278eeba2cffbd720b36c9e21a",
  "url": "https://github.com/example/project/commit/26aac9a2adb9a688ab8fe2a9664450de97557cf9.patch?full_index=1",
  "condition": {"op": "always"}
}
```

EasyBuild accepts HTTP(S) URLs in `patches` and checks the downloaded bytes
against the corresponding positional checksum. Local artifacts are verified
and copied into the recipe directory; remote artifacts remain URLs in the
emitted recipe. Imperative Spack `def patch(self)` methods cannot be represented
as patch files and become residual build-authoring work when their version
condition applies.

`easyconfig_parameters` accepts strings, integers, booleans, lists, and
tables. It cannot contain executable expressions. Build-level parameters are
defaults for every emitted recipe; profile-level parameters replace matching
keys for one variant.

# Planned CycloneDX SBOM

`package.sbom.cdx.json` is CycloneDX 1.5 derived from the package plan. It is a
pre-build inventory of requested components and dependency intent. It is not a
scan of installed files and does not establish the `builds` or
`binary-verified` claim.

The root component carries the primary source SHA-256 when available. Its
external references retain VCS tag/commit identity and one distribution URL
plus SHA-256 per source artifact, including derived GitHub tag archives. These
values come from the canonical plan after any explicit positional checksum
overrides.

Consumers should preserve the lifecycle and `eb_stack:*` properties when
copying the document into a wider stack report. Build evidence belongs in the
campaign state, not in the planned SBOM.

The planned SBOM omits a generation timestamp because its identity is the
canonical input and dependency intent, not the wall-clock time of a CLI run.
Campaign evidence records build and verification event times. This keeps the
SBOM reproducible across checkout roots and repeated planning runs.

# Product profiles and recipe names

A profile represents one loadable product. Each requested profile is solved
and emitted independently:

- the default profile has an empty versionsuffix and an unsuffixed recipe;
- a non-default profile declares its complete versionsuffix, such as
  `-complex`;
- Message Passing Interface (MPI) and OpenMP toolchain options alone do not create a separate recipe name;
- a feature or ABI variant that users load independently gets its own profile,
  lock, and `.eb` file.

For example, the QMCPACK profile set emits:

```text
locks/default.lock.json
locks/complex.lock.json
easyconfigs/q/QMCPACK/QMCPACK-4.3.0-foss-2026.1.eb
easyconfigs/q/QMCPACK/QMCPACK-4.3.0-foss-2026.1-complex.eb
```

# Resolvo profile lock

`locks/<profile>.lock.json` records the actual Boolean satisfiability (SAT) selection used to render
that recipe:

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "package": "QMCPACK",
  "version": "4.3.0",
  "profile": "complex",
  "toolchain": {"name": "foss", "version": "2026.1"},
  "versionsuffix": "-complex",
  "dependencies": [
    {
      "name": "HDF5",
      "version": "2.1.1",
      "toolchain": {"name": "foss", "version": "2026.1"},
      "easyconfig_path": "easybuild/easyconfigs/h/HDF5/HDF5-2.1.1-foss-2026.1.eb",
      "build": false
    }
  ],
  "pin_outcomes": [],
  "exclusions": [],
  "solver": "resolvo"
}
```

Every locked dependency carries its selected EasyBuild identity and source
recipe path. Standard robot trees retain the path beginning at
`easybuild/easyconfigs/`; other robot layouts retain the recipe filename.
Machine-local robot prefixes are not serialized. `build` distinguishes direct
build dependencies from runtime or host dependencies.

`pin_outcomes` keeps stack preferences reviewable. A `preferred` pin may record
`fallback: true` when Resolvo selects another jointly compatible candidate. A
`locked` pin cannot fall back. `exclusions` records candidates removed from
consideration with the evidence-backed reason and optional scope.

SAT compatibility is not build evidence. A selected candidate may still fail
configure, compile, link, tests, install, or sanity; the campaign records that
outcome as a typed finding.

# EasyBuild recipe set

Generated recipes follow the conventional EasyBuild hierarchy and syntax.
Sources and checksums remain positional: all source checksums precede patch
checksums. Verified local patch files are copied into the recipe directory;
checksum-addressed remote patches remain exact URLs. Robot overlays are
searched in command-line order, with later paths overriding earlier identities.

A foreign VCS commit is immutable source identity but is not the SHA-256 of
the downloaded archive. Supply one `--source-checksum` per source artifact when
the foreign recipe lacks archive hashes. `package inspect` keeps the missing
checksum as a blocking residual; `package plan` refuses to emit recipes until
all source and patch checksums are complete and valid.

Run the three recipe gates before a campaign:

```bash
eb-stack recipe format BUNDLE/easyconfigs/*/*/*.eb
eb-stack recipe lint BUNDLE/easyconfigs/*/*/*.eb
eb-stack recipe check \
  --recipe BUNDLE/easyconfigs/q/QMCPACK/QMCPACK-4.3.0-foss-2026.1.eb \
  --easyconfigs tests/sbom_recorded/cbc \
  --easyconfigs BUNDLE/easyconfigs
```

# Easyblocks included with the recipe

Some software cannot be described by an easyconfig alone. SeisSol's
`HOST_ARCH` sets the vector width of the kernels its code generators emit, so
it has to be derived from the build host at configure time, and the binary
name, and with it the sanity check, follows from that value. That logic
belongs in a software-specific easyblock, `EB_SeisSol`, not in a hardcoded
configure flag or a site hook.

A package layer keeps such an easyblock beside its easyconfigs:

```toml
[build]
easyblock = "EB_SeisSol"

[[build.easyblocks]]
filename = "seissol.py"
source = "easyblocks/seissol.py"
sha256 = "8c80992232a496096e6687679565509f2637d6cd2b03a0bbf49a3bc3a7488713"
```

`source` is relative to the layer file. A layer that sets `build.easyblocks`
owns the complete list. `build.drop_easyconfig_parameters` names the
parameters the easyblock derives itself, such as `sanity_check_paths`,
`test_cmd` or `modextrapaths`; they leave the build level and every
profile, so the emitted recipe carries none of them. Planning and bumping verify each module against its
SHA-256, parse it (without importing it), and record the classes it defines,
with their bases and `extra_options` keys, under `build.easyblocks` in the
plan. Planning fails when no included module defines the class the recipe
resolves to: the class named by `build.easyblock`, or the class EasyBuild
derives from the software name when none is named.

EasyBuild finds a software-specific easyblock by name, and its own easyconfigs
never spell it out, so when `build.easyblock` equals the derived class
(`EB_SeisSol` for SeisSol) the emitted recipe has no `easyblock` line.
The writer copies each module to `easyblocks/<letter>/<module>.py`, the layout
of the easyblocks repository. A campaign passes every module in that directory
to EasyBuild as `--include-easyblocks=FILE,FILE`, so the class exists for the
build without being installed first. `examples/packages/seissol-easyblock.toml`
layers this over `examples/packages/seissol.toml`.

The bundle establishes `resolves` only when every requested profile has a lock
and recipe. See [campaign state and findings](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/campaigns.html.md) for the build and binary claims.

# When a package owes an easyblock

A package that carries variant logic as data repeats that logic in every
recipe. A software-specific easyblock keeps it once, and the easyconfigs lean
on it. `package plan` and `package bump` decide whether a package owes one
when its recipe resolves to a generic easyblock: `build.easyblock` names none
or a class other than the one EasyBuild derives from the software name, and no
included module defines the derived class. Any one of three triggers applies:

1. Two or more profiles whose `config_options` differ from each other, after
   the build-level options. A variant switch such as QMCPACK's
   `-DQMC_COMPLEX`ON` against `-DQMC_COMPLEX`OFF` is this case.
2. The build-level or any profile `easyconfig_parameters` carry
   `sanity_check_paths`, `sanity_check_commands`, `test_cmd`, `testopts`,
   `pretestopts`, or `runtest` as a string command.
3. A profile's `sanity_check_paths.files` or `sanity_check_commands` names a
   binary that differs between profiles, as `qmcpack` and `qmcpack_complex` do.

The plan then records one residual. Its stage is `emit`, its category
`missing-easyblock`, its severity `judgment`, and its id
`missing-easyblock:<class>`, for example `missing-easyblock:EB_QMCPACK`. The
summary names the derived class. The evidence lists the profile option
differences, the parameters, and the binary names that would move into it.

`--emit-easyblock` on `package plan` and `package bump` (the `emit_easyblock`
argument of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools) renders a skeleton instead of leaving the residual:

```bash
eb-stack package plan --emit-easyblock \
  --source fixtures/foreign_ingest/spack_qmcpack/package.py \
  --package-config examples/packages/qmcpack.toml \
  --toolchain foss/2026.1 \
  --easyconfigs tests/sbom_recorded/cbc \
  --stack-policy policy.toml \
  --out-dir BUNDLE
```

The flag writes `easyblocks/<letter>/<module>.py` in the bundle, for QMCPACK
`easyblocks/q/qmcpack.py`, records it under `build.easyblocks` with its
SHA-256, and sets `build.easyblock` to the derived class, so no residual is
raised. The module derives from the plan's easyblock (`CMakeMake` when the
plan names none) and carries:

- one `CUSTOM` parameter per feature, with the default profile's value;
- a `configure_step` that passes the options present in the profiles where a
  feature is true and absent where it is false, and never overrides a
  `-D<option>=` already in `configopts`;
- a `test_step` when `test_cmd`, `testopts`, or `pretestopts` exist, which
  runs only when `runtest` is true;
- a `sanity_check_step` built from `sanity_check_paths` and
  `sanity_check_commands`, with a binary name that differs between profiles
  chosen by the feature that flips it;
- `make_module_extra` from `modextrapaths`.

The options the class sets leave the emitted recipes, which then select a
variant with a boolean parameter such as `complex = True`. Options shared by
every profile stay in the easyconfig. The recipes keep their test and sanity
parameters, so the skeleton and the recipes agree until a human moves them.

The module is a starting point. Its docstring says so, it has not been built,
and a human completes and reviews it before release. The rendered text
parses with the same reader that checks included modules, keeps lines within
120 characters, and carries the EasyBuild copyright header.
`examples/packages/easyblocks/qmcpack.py` shows a finished easyblock of this
shape. `package bump --emit-easyblock` writes the module and updates the plan
manifest; the retargeted recipe keeps the text of its source recipe. The flag
does not combine with package-closure planning.

# Build target configuration

A target routes one EasyBuild workload through four independent layers:
transport, executor, runtime, and EasyBuild settings. Target configuration is
public TOML files; site hostnames, paths, credentials, scheduler sizing, and private
images belong in a later site file.

# Layering model

Every file has `schema_version = 1` and one or more `[[targets]]` entries.
Files are applied in command-line order and entries merge by target name.

A later file replaces a complete named layer. It does not merge individual
fields inside that layer. If a site file supplies `[targets.runtime]`, that
block must contain the complete runtime configuration.

After layering, every target must have all four layers. Unknown fields and
unsupported schema versions fail loudly.

```bash
eb-stack target list \
  --config examples/targets/base.toml \
  --config examples/targets/site.example.toml

eb-stack target doctor \
  --config examples/targets/base.toml \
  --config examples/targets/site.example.toml \
  --target site-builder
```

`target doctor` independently executes transport, executor, runtime, and
EasyBuild probes. A reachable SSH host is not enough; all four checks must
succeed.

# Transport

| Kind | Required fields | Optional fields |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `local` | none | none |
| `ssh` | `host` | `port`, `command` (default `ssh`), `sync_command` (default `rsync`) |

SSH transport stages a bundle at
`<work_root>/bundles/<local-bundle-name>`. Commands are shell-quoted before
being passed to the remote host.

# Executor

| Kind | Required fields | Optional fields |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `direct` | none | none |
| `slurm` | none | `command`, `partition`, `account`, `cpus`, `memory`, `time`, `gres` |

The Slurm executor uses `srun` by default and routes both builds and binary
verification through the declared allocation. Bundle staging tests transport
without allocating a job.

# Runtime

| Kind | Required fields | Optional fields |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `host` | none | none |
| `podman` | `image` | `command`, `args`, `mounts`, `workdir` |
| `docker` | `image` | `command`, `args`, `mounts`, `workdir` |
| `eessi` | `storage` | `command` (default `eessi_container.sh`), `access` (default `ro`), `extra_bind_paths`, `resume` |

Container commands use `run --rm`, then runtime arguments, volume mounts, the
working directory, image, and routed workload. Every bundle, robot tree, work
root, temporary root, install prefix, and source cache referenced by the
workload must be visible inside the container.

The `eessi` runtime is the install backend for site/user/project overlays.
It launches `eessi_container.sh --mode exec`, fuse-mounts CernVM File System (CVMFS) inside the
image, and does not use the host CVMFS client. Plan `package plan --format pypi|cran`
on the host: the host `eb-stack` binary need not run in the
Debian 12 image. `scripts/eessi-extend-eb.sh` sources the European Environment for Scientific Software Installations (EESSI) init script, loads
`EESSI-extend`, and execs `eb`. See `examples/targets/eessi-extend.toml`.
Set exactly one of `EESSI_USER_INSTALL`, `EESSI_PROJECT_INSTALL`,
`EESSI_SITE_INSTALL`, or `EESSI_CVMFS_INSTALL` in
`[targets.easybuild.environment]`.

Compiled modules, build trees, and temporary files belong to one runtime ABI.
Do not reuse a host or different-image install prefix inside a container.
Source archives may share a cache because they contain no linked build output.

Cargo searches for `.cargo/config.toml` from its working directory through
parent directories. A container that bind-mounts a home directory can
therefore inherit host-only compiler wrappers or linkers. Put `work_root` in a
target-owned namespace that does not contain personal tool configuration.
Rust-backed recipes that intentionally disable wrappers must ~unset
RUSTC_WRAPPER CARGO_BUILD_RUSTC_WRAPPER~. Empty values remain present in the
environment, and Rust bootstrap can interpret the empty string as a wrapper
executable. The target-owned work root is what prevents `unset` from exposing
an inherited Cargo wrapper.

When site storage exists below a user's home directory, bind the target-owned
campaign directory into a neutral container path and use that path for both
`workdir` and `work_root`. The original home mount may remain available for
bundles and robot trees:

```toml
[targets.runtime]
mounts = [
  "/home/operator:/home/operator",
  "/home/operator/.local/share/eb-stack/targets/rocky9/campaigns:/eb-stack-campaigns",
]
workdir = "/eb-stack-campaigns"

[targets.easybuild]
work_root = "/eb-stack-campaigns"
```

Cargo invoked below `/eb-stack-campaigns/build` can discover only the target's
own closer configuration and cannot merge `/home/operator/.cargo/config.toml`.
This mount alias preserves the host storage location without leaking personal
linker flags into EasyBuild recipes.

# EasyBuild workload

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `command` | EasyBuild executable, usually `eb` |
| `robot_paths` | Ordered upstream and overlay easyconfig roots |
| `work_root` | Durable campaign and build root |
| `tmp_root` | `EASYBUILD_TMPDIR` for this target |
| `environment` | Environment passed to EasyBuild and verification commands |

The routed build command adds `--robot=<colon-separated paths>` and
`--buildpath=<work_root>/build`. Later robot roots override earlier recipes
with the same EasyBuild identity.

Treat `EASYBUILD_PARALLEL` and the executor allocation as one resource
contract. Parallel C++ compiler processes can each consume more than a
gigabyte, so CPU count alone is not a safe job count. The runnable local target
uses two parallel jobs for broad workstation compatibility; a site layer may
raise that value when its scheduler memory request or measured host headroom
supports it. If the kernel kills a compiler or the compiler reports exhausted
virtual memory, the campaign records a retryable `resource` finding. Lower the
parallelism or increase the executor allocation, then rerun the same campaign
state.

Do not place credentials in a public target file. Use an SSH agent, scheduler
credential mechanism, container registry login, or private site layer. Target
doctor and campaign state retain routed commands and compact output as evidence.

# Runnable local Rocky Linux target

The repository includes a complete local Podman target at
`examples/targets/local-podman.toml`. It uses one portable path namespace under
`/tmp/eb-stack`.

Build the image and prepare the mounted roots:

```bash
podman build -t eb-stack-rocky9 \
  -f skills/new-package/container/rocky9/Containerfile \
  skills/new-package/container/rocky9

mkdir -p \
  /tmp/eb-stack/robot \
  /tmp/eb-stack/overlay \
  /tmp/eb-stack/sources \
  /tmp/eb-stack/bundles

scripts/fetch-upstream-trees.sh
set -a
source "${EB_UPSTREAM_CACHE:-$HOME/.cache/eb-stack/upstream}/env.sh"
set +a
rsync -a "$EB_EASYCONFIGS"/ \
  /tmp/eb-stack/robot/
```

Probe the target:

```bash
eb-stack target doctor \
  --config examples/targets/local-podman.toml \
  --target local-rocky9
```

Write package bundles below `/tmp/eb-stack/bundles` so their absolute paths are
identical inside and outside the container. Then run a campaign:

```bash
eb-stack campaign run \
  --bundle /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon \
  --config examples/targets/local-podman.toml \
  --target local-rocky9 \
  --state /tmp/eb-stack/bundles/eon.campaign.json
```

The example enables the explicit EasyBuild and Message Passing Interface (MPI) root-container guards,
`TAR_OPTIONS=--no-same-owner`, and MPI yield-on-idle settings needed when test
suites oversubscribe the available cores. These settings keep the real build
and tests enabled; they do not bypass checks. Its conservative
`EASYBUILD_PARALLEL=2` default can be replaced in a private site layer after
the target's memory headroom is measured.

# Layered SSH, Slurm, and container target

Use `examples/targets/base.toml` as reusable topology and copy
`examples/targets/site.example.toml` to a private site file. The site layer can
replace transport with SSH, executor with Slurm, runtime with Podman or Docker,
and the complete EasyBuild workload with site-specific roots.

Validate the merged target with `target list` before doctoring it. This catches
misspelled target names and missing layers without starting a build.

# Campaign state and typed findings

A campaign turns a resolved package bundle into empirical build and binary
evidence on one named target. The JSON state is durable, resumable, and the
coordination surface for Hermes and OMP workers.

Hermes and OMP are role names rather than required orchestration software.
Hermes is the single campaign owner that classifies findings, applies or
coordinates repairs, and retries through the requested claim rung. OMP workers
are optional concurrent participants; their only shared coordination surface
is finding ownership in the campaign state.

# Run and inspect

```bash
eb-stack campaign run \
  --bundle BUNDLE \
  --config examples/targets/base.toml \
  --config examples/targets/site.example.toml \
  --target NAME \
  --state /tmp/campaign.json

eb-stack campaign status --state /tmp/campaign.json
```

`campaign run` is synchronous and stays in the foreground until every recipe
and verification command finishes or a typed failure is recorded. Run it under
the target site's terminal or service supervisor; `campaign status` remains
available from another process.

The state file has one writer while a run, claim, or resolution mutates it. An
OS-backed advisory guard enforces exclusivity, and the visible `.lock` file
records host, PID, and Linux process-start identity for diagnosis. The guard is
released by the operating system if the controlling process exits, so stale
metadata cannot permanently block a retry. Before retrying an interrupted run,
confirm that the routed container, scheduler job, or host command is no longer
active; a remote workload can outlive its controller. Reuse the same state
path. Package name and version must match, each run increments `attempts`,
history and findings remain available, and build/binary claims reset until the
current attempt proves them.

`campaign status` prints the complete audit record. Typed failures retain their
exact routed command, exit status, and compact evidence, including after their
findings are resolved or superseded. For a compact operator view during a long
build:

```bash
eb-stack campaign status --state /tmp/campaign.json |
  jq '{status, attempts, claims, current_recipe,
       active_findings: [.findings[] |
         select(.status == "open" or .status == "in-progress") |
         {id, class, stage, recipe, summary, owner}]}'
```

The campaign writes `status: running` and `current_recipe` before launching
EasyBuild, so another shell can observe those fields while the build command
is active. Keep the unfiltered state for diagnosis and handoff evidence.

# State schema

`CAMPAIGN.json` has `schema_version = 1`:

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "package": "QMCPACK",
  "version": "4.3.0",
  "bundle": "/work/qmcpack",
  "target": "site-builder",
  "status": "failed",
  "attempts": 2,
  "claims": {
    "resolves": true,
    "builds": false,
    "binary_verified": false
  },
  "findings": [],
  "history": []
}
```

Status is `planned`, `running`, `failed`, or `completed`. `current_recipe`
is present while an EasyBuild recipe is active and omitted otherwise.
History entries record the attempt, the status, an optional recipe path,
and a compact detail string.

# Claim ladder

The three booleans are independent claims:

1. `resolves`: every requested profile has a Resolvo lock and emitted recipe;
2. `builds`: every emitted recipe succeeds through EasyBuild on this target;
3. `binary_verified`: at least one verification command is declared and every
   declared command succeeds.

A completed campaign with no verification commands has `builds: true` and
`binary_verified: false`. A planned Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) never implies either build claim.

# Finding schema

A terminal failure appends a finding containing:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | Stable `attempt:N:finding:M` identity |
| `class` | Error-domain classification |
| `disposition` | Mechanical, retryable, judgment, or target repair |
| `stage` | `preflight`, `stage`, `build`, or `verify` |
| `recipe` | Relative recipe path or verification profile |
| `target` | Routed target name |
| `summary` / `evidence` | Compact diagnosis and terminal evidence |
| `command` / `exit_code` | Exact routed program, arguments, and exit status |
| `attempt` | Attempt that observed the failure |
| `status` / `owner` | Queue state and exclusive worker owner |
| `resolution` | Action, evidence, and changed paths |

Evidence contains the tail of routed stdout/stderr. When EasyBuild reports a
separate combined-output path, the campaign interns the nested log before
classification so the finding reflects the actual compiler or runtime error.

# Classes, dispositions, and repair surfaces

| Class | Default disposition | Start at |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `transport` | target-repair | SSH, rsync, host reachability, or staging path |
| `executor` | target-repair | Slurm command, partition, account, or allocation syntax |
| `runtime` | target-repair | Host/container executable, image, mounts, ABI, or environment |
| `interrupted` | retryable | Abandoned running state after the exclusive controller lock becomes available |
| `source` | requires-judgment | Upstream URL, mirror, source cache, or runtime network path |
| `checksum` | mechanical | Source digest and positional source/patch checksum list |
| `patch` | requires-judgment | Patch source, order, and applicability |
| `dependency-missing` | requires-judgment | Manifest, profile, stack policy, or real dependency recipe |
| `configure` | requires-judgment | Product options, detected dependency, toolchain, or patch |
| `compile` | requires-judgment | Source compatibility, compiler, flags, dependency, or patch |
| `link` | requires-judgment | Link interface, library order, ABI, or dependency selection |
| `test` | requires-judgment | Product behavior, test environment, or test-specific dependency |
| `install` | requires-judgment | EasyBuild install logic, paths, or permissions |
| `sanity` | requires-judgment | Sanity paths or profile verification command |
| `resource` | retryable | CPU, memory, GPU, filesystem, or scheduler sizing |
| `timeout` | retryable | Routed timeout or scheduler wall time |
| `unknown` | requires-judgment | Unclassified evidence; inspect the exact command and nested log |

The class narrows the first repair surface; it does not replace diagnosis.
For example, a SAT-compatible dependency that fails to compile remains a
`compile` finding until evidence supports a stack exclusion or package patch.
A compiler killed by the kernel, `virtual memory exhausted`, or equivalent
allocation evidence is instead a `resource` finding. Preserve the selected
dependency and recipe while correcting `EASYBUILD_PARALLEL` or the scheduler
allocation; only source-level compiler diagnostics justify a compile repair.

# Ownership protocol

Claim an open finding before changing state shared with another worker:

```bash
eb-stack campaign finding claim \
  --state /tmp/campaign.json \
  --id attempt:2:finding:1 \
  --owner omp-worker-1
```

Claims are exclusive. Reclaiming with the same owner is idempotent; a different
owner receives an ownership error.

Record the repair and its evidence:

```bash
eb-stack campaign finding resolve \
  --state /tmp/campaign.json \
  --id attempt:2:finding:1 \
  --owner omp-worker-1 \
  --action "corrected the container runtime environment" \
  --evidence "target doctor and the isolated command exit successfully" \
  --change examples/targets/site.example.toml
```

Run the campaign again with the same state. A successful retry marks matching
open or in-progress findings as `superseded` while retaining their evidence.
Resolved findings remain part of the audit trail.

# Repair loop

The task-oriented [campaign repair guide](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/../howto/repair-campaign.html.md) provides copyable commands and a
class-to-artifact troubleshooting table. The protocol is:

1. Run `target doctor` and the campaign.
2. Read the finding's stage, class, exact command, evidence, and nested log.
3. Reproduce the smallest failing command on the same target/runtime.
4. Claim the finding.
5. Change the layer supported by the evidence.
6. Run the nearest mechanical check: recipe lint/check, target doctor, or the
   isolated build command.
7. Resolve the finding with evidence and changed paths.
8. Rerun the full campaign state until every requested recipe and verification
   command succeeds.

Hermes owns this whole loop. OMP workers use finding ownership to divide
residual diagnosis without racing on the state file. The executable procedures
are [new package](https://github.com/HaoZeke/eb-stack/blob/main/skills/new-package/SKILL.md)
and [annual bump](https://github.com/HaoZeke/eb-stack/blob/main/skills/annual-bump/SKILL.md).

# Rust API

The public Rust API follows the version-one workflow rather than the retired
scaffold/auto-emitter surface.

# Canonical package modules

| Module | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `package` | schema-versioned plan, profiles, locks, stack policy, CycloneDX conversion |
| `package_config` | layered aliases, EasyBuild policy, and product profiles |
| `package_solve` | profile materialization and Resolvo lock generation |
| `package_emit` | one deterministic EasyBuild recipe per profile lock |
| `package_workflow` | inspect, new-package plan, bump plan, and bundle writer |

Primary entry points:

- `inspect_new_package`;
- `plan_new_package`;
- `plan_package_bump`;
- `write_package_bundle`;
- `solve_package_profile` / `solve_package_profile_with_hierarchy`;
- `emit_profile_easyconfigs`.

# Parsing and stack solving

`parse_foreign_path` and `parse_foreign_str` return the syntax-normalized
foreign model. `package_plan_from_foreign` is the canonical adapter.

`eb_parse` exposes EasyBuild parsing, robot tree merging, package gates, and
dependency checks. `resolvo_provider` implements candidate selection, policy
pins, stack preferences, locked pins, and exclusions. `select` provides the
whole-stack optimization path.

# Targets and campaigns

`target` exposes layered TOML types, target resolution, command plans, staging,
and target doctor reports. `campaign` exposes campaign state, typed findings,
claim/resolve operations, failure classification, and `run_campaign`.

# Generated API pages

The crate pages are generated from Rust source. The documentation build
appends them to this page.

```bash
pixi run -e docs gen-rust-api
```

# Policy JSON schema

A policy is the input that turns a universe of parsed easyconfig candidates
into one selection. It is a JSON object matching the `Policy` struct in
`src/domain.rs`.

# Full shape

```json
{
  "toolchain": {"name": "foss", "version": "2025b"},
  "roots": ["GROMACS"],
  "root_priority": ["GROMACS"],
  "pins": [
    {"name": "OpenBLAS", "version_req": "==0.3.24"}
  ],
  "forbid": ["OpenMPI-4.1.5-foss-2025b.eb"],
  "objective": "prefer_newer",
  "require_upgrade": {"name": "GROMACS", "relative_to_baseline": true}
}
```

Only `toolchain` and `roots` are required; every other field defaults as
noted below.

# Fields

- `toolchain` :: `{"name": string, "version": string}`. Required. Selects
  which candidates from the parsed tree participate: the policy toolchain,
  every member of its hierarchy, and `SYSTEM`. A recipe at `GCC` takes CMake
  from `GCCcore` and a licence file from `SYSTEM`, so an exact match on the
  policy toolchain alone cannot satisfy its own dependencies.
- `roots` :: Array of package names. Required, non-empty. Every dependency
  (runtime **and** build-time) a root needs co-selects automatically; the
  solve fails if any named root has no candidate at all.
- `root_priority` :: Optional array of package names. Declares which root
  wins the newest-version tie-break when two or more roots share a
  dependency with conflicting requirements. Defaults to `roots` list order
  when omitted or empty. Any root missing from an explicit
  `root_priority` is appended in `roots` order, so every root always
  participates. Reordering `roots` does **not** change the effective priority
  once `root_priority` is set explicitly. See
  [the how-to](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/../howto/root-priority.html.md) and
  [why this exists](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/../explanation/optimization-model.html.md).
- `pins` :: Optional array of `{"name": string, "version_req": string}`.
  Restricts a package to candidates whose version matches the requirement
  string (grammar below). A pin on a package with no matching candidate
  fails the solve at policy-construction time, before any Boolean satisfiability (SAT) solving
  happens.
- `forbid` :: Optional array of strings. Each entry matches either a full
  `easyconfig_path` or a bare package `name`; matching candidates are
  excluded from the universe entirely before solving.
- `prefer_installed` :: Optional bool, default false. When true, a package
  present in the baseline stays at that version unless a pin, a forbid, or
  `require_upgrade` says otherwise. The derived criteria are then
  `["-changed", "-notuptodate"]`: staying put outranks moving to newest.
- `objective` :: Optional string, default `"prefer_newer"`. The only
  objective the solver implements: among jointly feasible assignments,
  prefer the newest version of each root (in priority order), then the
  newest version of every other co-selected package.
- `criteria` :: Optional array of Common Upgradeability Description Format (CUDF) criterion names, in precedence
  order. Empty means derive them: `["-notuptodate"]` by default, or
  `["-changed", "-notuptodate"]` when `prefer_installed` is true. An
  explicit list wins. Known names are `-changed` (minimise packages moved
  off the baseline version) and `-notuptodate` (minimise packages held
  below the newest candidate). Any other name fails the solve. The applied
  list is recorded on the lock as `solver.criteria`.
- `require_upgrade` :: Optional ~{"name": string, "relative_to_baseline":
  bool}`, or an array of those objects. When `relative_to_baseline~ is
  true, the named package's solved version must be strictly newer than its
  version in the baseline lock (`--baseline-easyconfigs` or
  `--baseline-easystack`). No baseline, or no baseline entry for that
  package, fails the solve with an explicit error instead of skipping the
  requirement without a warning.

# version_req grammar

Used by both `pins[].version_req` and parsed easyconfig dependency
requirements (`=`X`, `>`X`, `<=X`, `>X`, `<X`, or a bare `X` for an exact
match). Version comparison is EasyBuild-shaped, not semver: digit runs
compare numerically, letter runs compare lexicographically, and a trailing
letter run with nothing on the other side sorts as a pre-release
(`2025a < 2025b`, `1.0rc1 < 1.0`).

# Effective root priority

```python
def effective_root_priority(policy):
    order = policy.root_priority or policy.roots
    order = [r for r in order if r in policy.roots]     # only real roots
    for r in policy.roots:
        if r not in order:
            order.append(r)                             # never drop a root
    return order
```

This is a description of `Policy::effective_root_priority` in
`src/domain.rs`, not a separate implementation; it is shown here because the
outcome of a multi-root solve depends entirely on this order.

# Where policies are consumed

- `eb-stack stack solve --stack-policy POLICY.json`

See
[how to solve a consistent stack lock](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/../howto/solve-lock.html.md).

# Output formats

# Stack lock (`stack.lock.json`)

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "toolchain": {"name": "foss", "version": "2025b"},
  "generation_label": "foss-2025b",
  "packages": [
    {
      "name": "GROMACS",
      "version": "2025.0",
      "toolchain": {"name": "foss", "version": "2025b"},
      "versionsuffix": null,
      "easyconfig_path": "foss-2025b/GROMACS-2025.0-foss-2025b.eb"
    }
  ],
    "solver": {
    "engine": "resolvo_cdcl_sat",
    "engine_version": "resolvo+eb_stack-0.3.0",
    "timestamp": "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z",
    "criteria": ["-notuptodate"]
  }
}
```

- `schema_version` :: `1`.
- `toolchain` :: The policy's target toolchain (not necessarily every
  package's own toolchain field, though in practice they match).
- `generation_label` :: Optional human label, e.g. `"foss-2025b"` when
  produced from an easyconfig tree. Library callers may omit it for hand-built
  universes.
- `packages` :: One entry per co-selected package, sorted by name. Each
  entry is a `LockPackage`: `name`, `version`, its own `toolchain`, optional
  `versionsuffix`, and the `easyconfig_path` it came from.
- `solver` :: `engine` is always `"resolvo_cdcl_sat"`. `engine_version`
  embeds the crate version. `timestamp` is RFC 3339 in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), second precision.
  `criteria` is the Common Upgradeability Description Format (CUDF) list the solve applied, in order. A policy that
  sets neither `criteria` nor `prefer_installed` records `["-notuptodate"]`.
  `prefer_installed` records `["-changed", "-notuptodate"]`. An explicit
  `criteria` list is recorded as written. See the
  [policy reference](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/policy.html.md).

# Internal candidate universe

```json
{
  "toolchain": {"name": "foss", "version": "2025b"},
  "generation_label": "foss-2025b",
  "candidates": [
    {
      "name": "GROMACS",
      "version": "2025.0",
      "toolchain": {"name": "foss", "version": "2025b"},
      "versionsuffix": null,
      "easyconfig_path": "foss-2025b/GROMACS-2025.0-foss-2025b.eb",
      "dependencies": [
        {"name": "OpenMPI", "version_req": "5.0.3"}
      ],
      "builddependencies": []
    }
  ]
}
```

`dependencies` and `builddependencies` use the same `DepReq` shape and the
same `version_req` grammar as policy pins (see
[policy reference](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/policy.html.md)). This structure is a Rust/library input;
the version-one CLI builds it from repeatable `--easyconfigs` paths.

# Build list (`--build-list-out`)

Plain text, one easyconfig path per line, trailing newline, no blank lines:

```text
fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025b/FFTW-3.3.10-foss-2025b.eb
fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025b/OpenBLAS-0.3.27-foss-2025b.eb
fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025b/OpenMPI-5.0.3-foss-2025b.eb
fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025b/Python-3.12.3-foss-2025b.eb
fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025b/GROMACS-2025.0-foss-2025b.eb
```

Order is a topological sort over the co-selected stack: a dependency's path
always appears before every co-selected package that needs it (runtime or
build-time). Ties are broken by package name for a deterministic order
independent of input list order or `HashMap` iteration. An empty lock
produces an empty file.

# Stack diff (`--stack-diff-out`)

Markdown, meant to be pasted directly into a pull request:

```markdown
# Stack diff

Baseline (`foss-2025a`) to solved (`foss-2025b`).

## Summary

- **unchanged**: 2
- **added**: 0
- **removed**: 0
- **version-bumped**: 3

## Packages

### FFTW: unchanged

- Baseline: `3.3.10` (`fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025a/FFTW-3.3.10-foss-2025a.eb`)
- Solved: `3.3.10` (`fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025b/FFTW-3.3.10-foss-2025b.eb`)

### GROMACS: version-bumped

- Baseline: `2024.1` (`fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025a/GROMACS-2024.1-foss-2025a.eb`)
- Solved: `2025.0` (`fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025b/GROMACS-2025.0-foss-2025b.eb`)
- Change: `2024.1` to `2025.0`

### OpenBLAS: version-bumped

- Baseline: `0.3.23` (`fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025a/OpenBLAS-0.3.23-foss-2025a.eb`)
- Solved: `0.3.27` (`fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025b/OpenBLAS-0.3.27-foss-2025b.eb`)
- Change: `0.3.23` to `0.3.27`

### OpenMPI: version-bumped

- Baseline: `4.1.5` (`fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025a/OpenMPI-4.1.5-foss-2025a.eb`)
- Solved: `5.0.3` (`fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025b/OpenMPI-5.0.3-foss-2025b.eb`)
- Change: `4.1.5` to `5.0.3`

### Python: unchanged

- Baseline: `3.12.3` (`fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025a/Python-3.12.3-foss-2025a.eb`)
- Solved: `3.12.3` (`fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs/foss-2025b/Python-3.12.3-foss-2025b.eb`)
```

Every package present in either the baseline or the solved lock is
classified once: `unchanged` (same version both sides), `added` (solved
only), `removed` (baseline only), or `version-bumped` (present both sides,
different version). Sections are sorted by package name.

# Planned Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) (`--sbom-out`, CycloneDX 1.5)

Documents are built with the official [cyclonedx-bom](https://crates.io/crates/cyclonedx-bom)
crate (same models as cargo-cyclonedx), serialized as CycloneDX 1.5 JSON.

Opt-in: `--sbom-out` has no default filename. Omit it and `stack solve` writes
only the lock (and any requested build list / stack diff). `eb-stack stack sbom --lock LOCK`
defaults to `stack.cdx.json` because that command's sole
purpose is SBOM emission.

```json
{
  "bomFormat": "CycloneDX",
  "specVersion": "1.5",
  "serialNumber": "urn:uuid:…",
  "version": 1,
  "metadata": {
    "timestamp": "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z",
    "tools": [{"vendor": "SURF", "name": "eb-stack", "version": "resolvo+eb_stack-0.3.0"}],
    "component": {
      "type": "application",
      "name": "easybuild-stack-foss-2025b",
      "version": "foss-2025b",
      "description": "Planned EasyBuild stack inventory from eb-stack lock (pre-install; not a post-build compliance scan)"
    },
    "lifecycles": [{"phase": "pre-build"}],
    "properties": [
      {"name": "eb_stack:document_kind", "value": "planned-sbom-from-lock"},
      {"name": "eb_stack:solver_engine", "value": "resolvo_cdcl_sat"},
      {"name": "eb_stack:toolchain", "value": "foss-2025b"}
    ]
  },
  "components": [
    {
      "type": "library",
      "bom-ref": "pkg:generic/GROMACS@2025.0?toolchain=foss-2025b",
      "name": "GROMACS",
      "version": "2025.0",
      "purl": "pkg:generic/GROMACS@2025.0?toolchain=foss-2025b",
      "properties": [
        {"name": "easybuild:toolchain", "value": "foss-2025b"},
        {"name": "easybuild:easyconfig_path", "value": "foss-2025b/GROMACS-2025.0-foss-2025b.eb"},
        {"name": "eb_stack:lifecycle", "value": "pre-install-plan"}
      ]
    }
  ],
  "dependencies": [
    {"ref": "pkg:generic/GROMACS@2025.0?toolchain=foss-2025b", "dependsOn": ["pkg:generic/Python@3.12.3?toolchain=foss-2025b", "pkg:generic/OpenBLAS@0.3.27?toolchain=foss-2025b", "pkg:generic/OpenMPI@5.0.3?toolchain=foss-2025b", "pkg:generic/FFTW@3.3.10?toolchain=foss-2025b"]}
  ]
}
```

Each component's `bom-ref` / `purl` is a synthetic `pkg:generic/` reference
(EasyBuild has no dedicated Package URL (purl) type) embedding name, version, and
toolchain. Metadata `lifecycles: pre-build` and
`eb_stack:lifecycle: pre-install-plan` mark a **planned** inventory from the
solver selection, not a scan of installed software.

`dependsOn` edges:

- From `stack solve --sbom-out`, `eb-stack stack sbom --lock LOCK`, and
  the Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool `eb_stack_sbom`: each package's declared runtime
  `dependencies`, intersected with co-selected lock members, read from
  the easyconfigs the lock names. Checksums and source URLs come from
  those recipes too. Build-time deps (`builddependencies`) go on the
  component property `eb_stack:buildDependsOn` (comma-separated refs),
  not the runtime graph.
  A relative `easyconfig_path` is the recipe beside the lock file when
  that file exists, and otherwise the same path against the process
  directory. An unreadable path contributes no edges. The document does
  not invent all-to-all co-stack cycles. `stack sbom` and
  `eb_stack_sbom` report how many recipes were read. Empty `dependsOn`
  arrays may be omitted by cyclonedx-bom serialization.

# Build order (`stack order --out`)

One easyconfig path per line, in dependency order. A generation that
builds one name twice lists both paths. `--oldest` changes which unpinned
version is chosen; it does not change the file shape.

Stdout names a repeated build as `multiple builds of <name>: <ver-tc>, ...`
and ends with `order`<path> builds`<N>`.

# Input hashes (`--hashes-out`)

One line per module, two spaces between the fields, the same layout as
`sha256sum`:

```text
0123abcd...  GROMACS-2025.0-foss-2025b
```

The digest covers the easyconfig bytes and the hashes of everything that
module needs (`eb-stack-input-v1`). A recipe that cannot be read still
gets a line. Stdout reports `incomplete=` as how many of those lines are
not a complete closure.

# Easystack (`stack easystack`, `--easystack-out`)

YAML with one `easyconfigs` list. A filename with no options is a string.
A filename with `--option` values is a mapping:

```yaml
easyconfigs:
- OpenMPI-5.0.7-GCC-14.2.0.eb
- CUDA-12.8.0.eb:
    options:
      accept-eula-for: CUDA
```

`stack order --easystack-out` writes the build sequence. `stack easystack`
writes lock order, which is sorted by package name.

# Jenkins sections (`stack sections`)

The same build-list lines as the input, regrouped under `#### Title ####`
headers taken from `--from`. Commented-out lines stay commented out.
Packages the previous list does not name go under the `--unfiled` header.

# Source fetch (`sources.fetch.json`)

Written by `package bump --fetch-checksums` when at least one source was
considered. A JSON array:

```json
[
  {
    "filename": "app-1.1.tar.gz",
    "url": "https://example.invalid/app-1.1.tar.gz",
    "sha256": "0123abcd",
    "errors": []
  }
]
```

`url` and `sha256` are omitted when there is nothing to report. `errors`
is omitted when the download succeeded. The downloaded bytes are not
stored in this file.

# Reproduction scores (`repro summary`)

`--scores` is a directory of one `<case>.json` per case. `--json` prints
that array. Each object has `case`, `pull_request` (a number or null),
`source`, `target`, `score` (`EXACT`, `SEMANTIC`, or `MATERIAL`),
`allowance` (lines forgiven), `stale_allowance`, and `residual_lines`.
A stale entry is `{"kind": "absent_from_target", "line": "..."}` or
`{"kind": "already_emitted", "line": "..."}`.

The table form is fixed:

```text
| Case | PR | Score | Allowance | Residual |
|---+---+---+---+---|
```

`--ratchet` reads `note`, `cases` (case name to allowance count), and
`total`. `total` has to equal the sum of `cases`.

# Pull-request build set (`eb-stack pr-overlap`)

One run writes three files. `prs/<N>.toml` is the SBOM for pull request `N`:
the closure of the easystack entries it adds, minus modules already
installed. `overlap.toml` is the same build sets intersected. `overlap.md` is
that intersection as a report. Every file starts with the never-merge header.

`to_build` is one sorted module per line, so the same line in two
`prs/<N>.toml` files is a module both pull requests would build.
`sort | uniq -d` on those lines, and a staging merge of the files, are the
overlap report.

## `prs/<N>.toml`

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `schema_version` | `1` |
| `pr` | Pull request number |
| `head_sha` | Head commit the record was computed for |
| `title` | Title at that commit, omitted when unknown |
| `generated_at` | RFC 3339 timestamp of the run |
| `eessi_version` | Stack version, from `--eessi-version` |
| `installed_source` | Label of the installed list |
| `easystack_files` | Easystack paths that contributed an entry |
| `to_build` | Module names that would be built, sorted, one per line |
| `already_installed` | Installed modules the walk reached and stopped at, sorted |
| `unresolved` | Requirements no easyconfig on the robot path satisfies, and `easyblock <class> missing` when `--easyblocks` was passed and no passed tree defines that class |
| `notes` | Present when the run recorded one: a class supplied by an `include-easyblocks-from-commit` tree, a commit an entry names whose tree was not passed, or an `include-easyblocks-from-pr`. Omitted when empty |
| `entries` | The easystack lines the pull request adds |

A module whose easyblock class is missing is left out of `to_build`. The
dependencies of that recipe stay. `overlap.md` prints each unresolved item
as `- unresolved:` and each note as `- note:`.

Each `[[entries]]` table has `easystack`, `easyconfig`, and, when the entry
carries them, `from_commit` and `eb_version`. A module name is
`name/version[-toolchain]versionsuffix`, with the system toolchain omitted.

`[[revisions]]` is each easystack or easyconfig file the pull request
changes. `kind` is `easystack` or `easyconfig`. `base` and `head` are the
file text when the fetch stored it. `base_blob` and `head_blob` are the git
blob ids of those bytes. A later merge-order reads this text, so the hunk
check does not need the original JSON. Omitted when the run stored none.

A worked record from an open 2026.06 pull request is in
[from one easystack line to a build set](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/../explanation/pr-overlap.html.md).

## `overlap.toml`

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `schema_version` | `1` |
| `generated_at` | Same timestamp as the records |
| `eessi_version` | Stack version |
| `installed_source` | Label of the installed list |
| `prs` | Pull request numbers that received a record, ascending |
| `shared` | Module to the pull requests that would build it, for modules more than one would build |
| `pairs` | Per pull request, the other pull requests it shares modules with, and which modules |

## `overlap.md`

The same `shared` map as a table, then one section per pull request: how
many modules it builds, which other open pull requests it shares them with,
and any unresolved requirements. Pull requests are written as `#N` text when
`--repo-url` is empty, and as links otherwise. The flag defaults to
`https://github.com/EESSI/software-layer`. The file links on GitHub without adding
an entry to a pull request timeline.

## `merge-order.toml`

Written only with `--merge-order` (or `--merged`, which turns that flag
on). The same never-merge header. Schema `1`.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `schema_version` | `1` |
| `generated_at` | Same timestamp as the overlap index |
| `installed_source` | Label of the installed list |
| `merged` | `--merged` numbers, ascending. Empty when the flag is absent |
| `steps` | One step per pull request that is not in `merged` |
| `cycles` | Strongly connected sets. Each set is sorted, and the sets are sorted |
| `conflicts` | Easystack paths edited by two or more pull requests in a colliding way |

Each `[[steps]]` table:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `position` | 1-based index in `steps` |
| `pr` | Pull request number |
| `after` | Direct predecessors in the binding graph, ascending |
| `builds` | Residual `to_build` once every earlier step has merged, sorted |
| `saves` | Later pull requests, and the modules they no longer build |
| `reason` | Why this pull request was picked |

`saves` is `[[steps.saves]]` with `pr` and `modules`. A conflict has
`easystack`, `prs`, and `kind`. `kind` is `same-insertion` or `same-entry`.

With `--merge-order`, `overlap.md` gains a Merge order table: position,
pull request, build count, saves, and after. Conflicts follow that table
when any were found. Without the flag the Markdown file is unchanged.

## `merge-impact.toml`

Written only when `--impact` is passed. The same never-merge header.
Schema `1`. This is not the residual after earlier steps of
`merge-order.toml`. The named pull request's `to_build` counts as newly
installed, after the modules of every `--merged` pull request are
removed. Those pull requests are left out of `affected`. `--impact N`
when N is also `--merged` is an error:
`--impact N: already listed in --merged`.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `schema_version` | `1` |
| `generated_at` | Same timestamp as the overlap index |
| `impacts` | One entry per requested pull request, in ascending number order |

Each `[[impacts]]` table has `pr` and `affected`. Each `[[impacts.affected]]`
table:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `pr` | Another pull request whose build set or depends-on edge changes |
| `shrinks` | Modules that leave that pull request's `to_build`, sorted |
| `resolves` | Modules of a depends-on edge from the named pull request. It asks for the module by name, and the other only reaches it. Both asking is not an edge |

An unknown number is an error before the file is written:
`--impact N: no pull request with that number`. An unknown `--merged`
number is the same kind of error. A number that is in the input but
changes no easyconfig and no easystack is
`pull request N has no record (no easyconfigs or easystack change)`.
Neither one creates the output
directory or deletes files already in it. For an easyconfigs run,
`resolves` lists the modules on a `depends-on` row from the named pull
request, including a module it patches when another pull request builds
a dependent of that module. `shrinks` is the shared `to_build` that
remains after `--merged` modules are removed. Modules from a
`depends-on` row into the pull request are excluded from `shrinks`. A
software-layer `resolves` list is the modules the named pull request
asks for by easystack entry.

## Easyconfigs records (schema 2)

`--kind easyconfigs` writes schema 2. A software-layer record stays schema
1 and omits the fields below. `eessi_version` is omitted when it is empty.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `schema_version` | `2` |
| `kind` | `easyconfigs` |
| `changed_easyconfigs` | One entry per `.eb` path: `path`, `status` (`added`, `modified`, or `deleted`), and `module` when the file parses |
| `closure` | Every module the changed easyconfigs reach, sorted, including the pull request's own modules |
| `new_modules` | Closure modules the base tree does not provide |
| `reverse_dependents` | Base-tree modules that depend on a modified or deleted file of this pull request. Each entry has `module`, `depth`, and `class`. Depth 1 depends on the file itself. `class` is `must-rebuild`, `review`, or `no-rebuild`, the same three classes as `rebuild-set.json`. A bundle whose `exts_list` names the patched package is `must-rebuild`. A runtime dependency is `no-rebuild`. A dependent reached only through builddependencies is `review`. A toolchain edge is not listed. `overlap.md` prints the module, the depth, and the class |
| `to_build` | Closure minus `--installed` when that flag is set; otherwise the same modules as `new_modules`. A modified easyconfig, and every reverse dependent classed `must-rebuild`, is included even when that module is installed or already in the base tree. `review` and `no-rebuild` stay out of `to_build` and stay on `reverse_dependents`. A deleted easyconfig is not built. Merge order and `--impact` schedule this list |

The other pull requests in the same run are on the robot path while
resolving, between the base tree and this pull request's own files.
`new_modules` is still compared to the base tree alone.
`--filter-deps` is applied to a copy of the base tree before the reverse
walk. A dependency it drops is not a reverse dependent and does not create
a `depends-on` row.

`overlap.toml` for this kind is schema 2 and adds `rows`. There are 4
kinds:

| `kind` | When it is written |
| --- | --- |
| `same-file` | 2 pull requests change one path. `path` is that path. `prs` lists the numbers |
| `same-module` | 2 pull requests add easyconfigs for one module. `module` is that module |
| `shared-new-module` | One module is in 2 pull requests' `new_modules` |
| `depends-on` | Pull request `to` reaches a module pull request `from` adds, `to` does not also add it, and the module is in `from`'s `new_modules`. A file `from` adds for a module the base tree already provides is not a dependency. The same row is written when `from` modifies or deletes a module and `to` builds a dependent of it: the module is in `to`'s closure, or `to`'s `to_build` contains one of `from`'s reverse dependents, and `to` does not itself change that module. `modules` lists the added or patched modules. `merge-order.toml` orders `from` before `to` |

A software-layer index stays schema 1 and omits `rows`.

# Rebuild set (`eb-stack rebuild-set`)

One run writes `rebuild-set.json`, `rebuild-set.md`, and one easystack per
EasyBuild version under `rebuilds/`. The date in the easystack filename is
the `YYYYMMDD` taken from `generated_at`. The version is the newest
EasyBuild version among the easystacks whose closure contains that
must-rebuild module, read from `-eb-` in the easystack filename. When no
filename carried a version, the file is `unknown`.

## `rebuild-set.json`

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `schema_version` | `4` |
| `generated_at` | RFC 3339 timestamp of the run |
| `installed_source` | Label of the installed list |
| `prefix` | Installed prefix passed to `--prefix`. Omitted when the flag was not passed |
| `symbols_checked` | `true` when `--check-static` ran |
| `easystacks` | Easystack paths that were read, sorted |
| `changed` | Patched easyconfig filenames, sorted |
| `missing` | Changed filenames that are not in the deployed graph |
| `unresolved` | Requirements no easyconfig satisfies, and easystack entries the robot path does not have |
| `notes` | A missing easyblock class, a `from-commit` whose tree was not given, or an install directory that was not found. Empty when there is nothing to say |
| `counts` | Row counts, with keys `no-rebuild`, `review`, and `must-rebuild` |
| `rows` | Installed reverse dependents. A review dependent is one row. The other classes stay one row per edge |

Each row has `changed`, `dependent`, `dependent_easyconfig`, `edge_kind`
(`changed`, `runtime`, `builddependency`, or `extension`), `class`
(`no-rebuild`, `review`, or `must-rebuild`), `reason`, and `eb_version`
when an easystack filename carried one. On a review row, `changed` is the
patched filenames joined by `, `. After `--check-static`, a hit keeps only
the filenames whose exports were defined.

`rebuild-set.md` is the same rows as a table, the counts line, the missing
filenames, and each note as `- note:`.

## `rebuilds/<YYYYMMDD>-eb-<version>-cve-patches.yml`

Class `must-rebuild` only. Entries are sorted by filename. `rebuild: true`
is set because the module is already installed.

```yaml
# In-place patches, same filename and version.
# Class must-rebuild only: the patched easyconfig, a bundle that includes it as an extension,
# and, when --check-static was used, a dependent that defines an export of the patched library.
# Generated by `eb-stack rebuild-set`.
easyconfigs:
  - Bundle-1.0-GCCcore-15.2.0.eb:
      options:
        rebuild: true
```

A worked classification is in
[what an in-place patch forces a rebuild of](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/../explanation/rebuild-set.html.md).

# Component reach (`eb-stack component-reach`)

One run writes `component-reach.toml`, `component-reach.json`, and
`component-reach.md`. The TOML file starts with
`# Generated by `eb-stack component-reach`.`

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `schema_version` | `1` |
| `generated_at` | RFC 3339 timestamp of the run |
| `component` | Name that was asked for |
| `version_req` | Exact version, `*`, or a requirement. Empty when the match is only `versions` |
| `version_reqs` | Present when more than one requirement was OR-ed. Any one of them matches |
| `versions` | Exact versions from a Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) record, present when the list is not empty |
| `purl` | Package URL, when the query was a purl or a resolved CVE |
| `ecosystem` | Ecosystem from the purl or the Open Source Vulnerabilities (OSV) record |
| `generation` | Toolchain generation |
| `carriers` | Easyconfigs and modules that carry it |
| `changed` | Filenames that contain it, fed to the closure |
| `closure_counts` | Row counts, keys `no-rebuild`, `review`, `must-rebuild` |
| `closure_rows` | Rebuild-set rows for `changed` |
| `missing` | Changed filenames absent from the closure graph |
| `notes` | A compat-layer hit, or a note the closure recorded |

`version_reqs`, `versions`, `purl`, and `ecosystem` are omitted when
empty, so a `--component` run stays the same shape as before.

Each carrier has `role` (`module`, `dependency`, `builddependency`,
`component`, `extension`, `crate`, `wheel`, `source`, `patch`,
`compat-layer`, or `installed`), `version`, `easyconfig` (empty for
compat-layer and installed-only rows), `module`, and `installed` when a
list was passed.

A `--cve` run writes the same three filenames with a different document.
`kind` is `cve`. `cve` is the id. `resolved` is the packages OSV named
(`ecosystem`, `name`, `purl`, `version_reqs`, `versions`). `results` is
one component-reach document per package. `notes` contains alias fetches
that failed. Schema version stays `1`.

A closure row has the rebuild-set fields `changed`, `dependent`,
`dependent_easyconfig`, `edge_kind`, `class`, `reason`, and `eb_version`
when an easystack filename carried one. With no easystack the synthetic
stack is `generation-<generation>.yml` and `eb_version` is absent.

`component-reach.md` is the carrier table, then the closure table, the
counts line, and each note as `- note:`.

# From recipe to verified package

The lifecycle has three claims. Treating them as one is the main source of
incorrect status reports.

```dot
digraph C {
  graph [fontname="Jost", fontsize=12, rankdir=TB, splines=true, bgcolor="transparent"];
  node  [fontname="Jost", fontsize=12, shape=box, style="rounded,filled",
         fillcolor="white", color="#004D40", fontcolor="#004D40"];
  edge  [fontname="Jost", fontsize=11, color="#004D40"];

  inspect [label="package inspect\n(no claim)"];
  plan    [label="package plan / package bump\n→ resolves", fillcolor="#F1DB4B", fontcolor="#004D40"];
  build   [label="campaign run\n→ builds", fillcolor="#004D40", fontcolor="white"];
  verify  [label="profile verification commands\n→ binary-verified", fillcolor="#FF655D", fontcolor="white"];

  inspect -> plan [style=dashed, label="no rung"];
  plan -> build [label="target + EasyBuild"];
  build -> verify [label="declared checks"];
}
```

# Claim 1: resolves

A package resolves when every requested profile has:

- a validated canonical manifest and planned Software Bill of Materials (SBOM);
- a jointly feasible Resolvo lock under the selected hierarchy and stack policy;
- a deterministic EasyBuild recipe generated from that lock.

`package plan` and `package bump` can establish this claim. `package inspect`
cannot, because it has no lock or recipe.

Resolution catches missing candidates, incompatible constraints, locked pin
violations, known exclusions, hierarchy mistakes, and invalid recipe metadata.
It does not download or compile software.

# Claim 2: builds

A package builds when every emitted recipe completes through EasyBuild on the
configured target. This exercises source downloads, checksums, patches,
configure, compile, link, tests, install, and EasyBuild sanity checks.

Only `campaign run` can establish this claim. A version range or prior recipe
is not build evidence for a new toolchain, platform, runtime, or product
profile.

# Claim 3: binary-verified

A package is binary-verified when all verification commands declared by its
profiles succeed after the EasyBuild recipes build. These commands can load the
module, invoke binaries, inspect versions/features, or perform site-specific
run-time search path (RPATH)/link checks.

A campaign with no verification commands may establish **builds** but leaves
**binary-verified** false.

# Lifecycle sequence

1. Parse the foreign or EasyBuild source into `PackagePlan`.
2. Review the planned SBOM and residuals.
3. Materialize each product profile.
4. Apply stack preferences/exclusions inside Resolvo and write locks.
5. Emit one conventional EasyBuild recipe per profile.
6. Format, lint, and robot-check the recipes.
7. Resolve target layers and probe them with `target doctor`.
8. Run the campaign on the EasyBuild host/runtime.
9. Claim, repair, and resolve typed findings; rerun the same state.
10. Hand the recipe set and evidence to the human operator for repository/PR
    publication.

# Repair ownership

- Parser/provenance defects belong in package-agnostic syntax adapters.
- Foreign-to-EasyBuild aliases, package/build policy, and product choices belong
  in package TOML.
- Distribution/site versions and known bad candidates belong in stack policy.
- Mechanical version selection belongs in Resolvo.
- Recipe syntax, checksums, patches, build logic, and sanity paths belong in the
  generated/authored easyconfig.
- Host, scheduler, runtime, paths, modules, and environment belong in target
  configuration.
- Empirical failures and repair evidence belong in campaign state.

This structure lets Hermes own the build-evaluation loop without turning every
failure into unstructured prompt text. OMP workers can coordinate by finding
class and ownership while preserving the exact command and evidence.

# Architecture

`eb-stack` separates package intent, dependency selection, recipe emission,
and empirical build evidence. Every user-facing workflow passes through the
same canonical package model.

# Data flow

```dot
digraph P {
  graph [fontname="Jost", fontsize=12, rankdir=LR, splines=true, bgcolor="transparent"];
  node  [fontname="Jost", fontsize=12, shape=box, style="rounded,filled",
         fillcolor="white", color="#004D40", fontcolor="#004D40"];
  edge  [fontname="Jost", fontsize=11, color="#004D40"];

  foreign   [label="conda-forge / Spack\nsyntax adapters"];
  easybuild [label="EasyBuild recipe\nadapter"];
  plan      [label="PackagePlan\npackage.plan.json", fillcolor="#F1DB4B"];
  sbom      [label="planned CycloneDX"];
  profile   [label="profile materialization"];
  resolvo   [label="stack policy + Resolvo", fillcolor="#004D40", fontcolor="white"];
  lock      [label="profile lock"];
```
