```dot
  emit      [label="one .eb per profile"];
  target    [label="transport + executor\n+ runtime + workload"];
  campaign  [label="campaign state\n+ typed findings", fillcolor="#FF655D", fontcolor="white"];

  foreign -> plan;
  easybuild -> plan;
  plan -> sbom;
  plan -> profile -> resolvo -> lock -> emit -> target -> campaign;
}
```

# Command surface

CLI namespaces and matching Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools share one workflow graph:

```dot
digraph S {
  graph [fontname="Jost", fontsize=12, rankdir=LR, splines=true, bgcolor="transparent"];
  node  [fontname="Jost", fontsize=11, shape=box, style="rounded,filled",
         fillcolor="white", color="#004D40", fontcolor="#004D40"];
  edge  [fontname="Jost", fontsize=10, color="#004D40"];

  package  [label="package\ninspect · plan · bump", fillcolor="#F1DB4B"];
  recipe   [label="recipe\neasyblock · templates · hierarchy\ncheck · lint · format"];
  stack    [label="stack\nsolve · sbom · order\neasystack · sections"];
  target   [label="target\nlist · doctor"];
  campaign [label="campaign\nrun · status · finding", fillcolor="#FF655D", fontcolor="white"];
  repro    [label="repro\nsummary"];
  mcp      [label="mcp stdio\neb_* tools", fillcolor="#004D40", fontcolor="white"];

  package -> recipe -> stack;
  stack -> target -> campaign;
  campaign -> repro;
  package -> mcp [style=dashed];
  recipe -> mcp [style=dashed];
  stack -> mcp [style=dashed];
  target -> mcp [style=dashed];
  campaign -> mcp [style=dashed];
  repro -> mcp [style=dashed];
}
```

# Syntax adapters

The conda adapter expands a restricted template subset, parses classic and v1
recipe shapes, preserves multi-source entries, and represents selectors as
structured conditions. The Spack adapter statically reads package domain-specific language (DSL) calls;
it does not execute Python. A Python abstract syntax tree (AST) evaluator handles literal assignments,
collections, bounded loops, static conditionals, formatting, and nested
`with when(...)` scopes. It preserves versions, dependencies and roles,
variants, conflicts, requirements, source metadata, and source spans.

A directive enters the canonical model only when its arguments evaluate to
static values. Unsupported expressions become source-located residuals instead
of partial strings or guessed facts.

Adapters also emit informational notes about successful normalization. Notes
never determine whether work remains: only structured residual records cross
into the canonical plan and campaign queue. This keeps language used in a
diagnostic from changing build behavior.

Adapters do not choose EasyBuild dependency versions or emit placeholder
recipes. Their output is package intent plus explicit residuals.

# Provider mapping

Layered package policy maps foreign dependency identities to EasyBuild
providers after syntax parsing. Direct aliases preserve constraints when the
two ecosystems use the same version domain. Component-to-provider aliases can
drop a component constraint that has no meaning for the containing provider.
The mapping is data, not parser control flow, and dependency provenance keeps
the foreign evidence available for review.

# Canonical package model

`PackagePlan` is schema-versioned and shared by foreign imports and bumps. It
contains package metadata, provenance-bearing sources and dependencies,
structured conditions/rules, EasyBuild build intent, product profiles, output
requests, and residuals.

The planned Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) is derived from this model. It is marked pre-build and remains
separate from installed/binary evidence.

# Product profiles

Profiles represent independently installable products. Materialization applies
feature flags, dependency-feature values, compiler/toolchain/platform context,
variables, versionsuffix components, toolchain options, configuration options,
and verification commands.

The emission invariant is one profile lock and one conventional `.eb` file per
requested profile. The default CPU product, with Message Passing Interface (MPI) and OpenMP, is unsuffixed unless the
site explicitly defines a distinct loadable variant.

# Resolvo boundary

The solver receives:

- the materialized direct dependency requirements;
- candidates filtered through the EasyBuild toolchain hierarchy;
- preferred or locked stack pins;
- candidate exclusions backed by target/build evidence.

Preferred pins use Resolvo's favored candidate and retain an in-solver
fallback. Locked pins constrain selection to one candidate. Pin outcomes and
exclusions are serialized in the profile lock.

Existing robot recipes are already-built artifacts. Their build-only tools
have independent build contexts and are not forced into the generated
package's co-loaded runtime closure. Direct build requirements of the generated
profile remain solver requirements and are emitted as build dependencies.

`exts_list` entries become virtual candidates (`easyconfig_path` contains
`#ext:`) that depend on the parent bundle. A requirement for `numpy` is
therefore satisfied by selecting `SciPy-bundle`. Profile locks collapse the
provide to the parent so emission never writes a standalone `numpy`
dependency tuple. The expansion is idempotent and runs inside Resolvo
admission, so `unsatisfied_direct_dependencies` sees the same universe.

# Deterministic EasyBuild emission

New-package emission renders package metadata, all sources and checksums,
EasyBuild build settings, locked dependency tuples, profile toolchain options,
configuration, sanity paths, and module class. Bumps preserve the source
recipe's syntax and unrelated bytes while applying the canonical lock to the
toolchain, package version, dependency versions, and source checksum entry.

# Layered targets

A target is four orthogonal layers:

1. transport: local or SSH;
2. executor: direct or Slurm;
3. runtime: host, Podman, or Docker;
4. EasyBuild workload: command, robot paths, durable roots, and environment.

TOML layers merge by target name in argument order. This keeps the public
repository and skills portable while a private site layer supplies hostnames,
paths, modules, scheduler sizing, and container images.

Compiled EasyBuild modules, work trees, and temporary roots belong to one
runtime ABI. A container target therefore uses its own `EASYBUILD_INSTALLPATH`,
`work_root`, and `tmp_root`. Source archives may use a shared cache because they
do not contain host-linked executables.

# Persisted campaigns

A campaign stages one bundle, builds every emitted recipe, and runs profile
verification commands. Its state stores attempts, exact routed commands,
compact evidence, typed findings, ownership, resolutions, and the three claims.

Spawn, controller interruption, and exit failures are data, not lost control
flow. They are classified as transport, executor, runtime, interrupted,
checksum, patch, dependency, configure, compile, link, test, install, sanity,
resource, timeout, or unknown findings. Hermes drives retries; OMP workers
coordinate through claim/resolve operations.

# API surface

The CLI and MCP server expose the same version-one workflows. Internal parser
and syntax-preserving emit modules are not compatibility APIs. There is one
canonical route for new packages and one for bumps, both ending in the same
bundle and campaign model.

# The optimization model

`eb-stack` uses [resolvo](https://github.com/mamba-org/resolvo), a conflict-driven clause learning (CDCL) Boolean satisfiability (SAT)
solver, as its feasibility core. CDCL SAT answers one question well: *does a
consistent assignment exist* under the requirements given. It does not, by
itself, answer **which** consistent assignment is best when more than one
exists and a policy has more than one root. `eb-stack` adds a small
optimization layer on top of feasibility to answer that second question
deterministically.

# Why feasibility alone is not enough

resolvo's own candidate ordering
(`resolvo_provider::EbProvider::sort_candidates`) sorts each **individual**
package's candidates newest-first, so the solver's internal search leans
toward newer versions. That is a per-package heuristic for the SAT search,
not a joint, policy-aware optimum across every root. With a single root, the
newest jointly-feasible version and the heuristic's pick coincide, because
there is only one root to satisfy. With two or more roots that share a
dependency and disagree about its version, "which root's newest version
wins" is not determined by that heuristic: it can depend on incidental input
order rather than anything a policy author declared.

# A conflict between two roots

```python
# GROMACS's newest easyconfig
dependencies = [('OpenMPI', '==4.1.6')]

# LAMMPS's newest easyconfig
dependencies = [('OpenMPI', '>=5.0.3')]
```

Only one `OpenMPI` version is co-selected per lock, so `GROMACS`'s newest
and `LAMMPS`'s newest cannot both be selected: whichever root keeps its
newest version forces the other one down to whatever version of it is
compatible with the winning `OpenMPI`. Plain feasibility says "a solution
exists"; it does not say which root's newest version that solution should
favor. See [the how-to](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/../howto/root-priority.html.md) for this exact
fixture solved both ways.

# The priority-lexicographic layer

`solve_with_resolvo` (in `resolvo_provider.rs`) resolves the ambiguity with
sequential lexicographic maximization over
`Policy::effective_root_priority`: fix the highest-priority root's version
first, keep it fixed, move to the next root.

```dot
digraph G {
    rankdir=TB;
    node [shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="white", fontname="Jost", fontsize=12];
    edge [fontname="Jost", fontsize=11, color="#004D40"];
    graph [fontname="Jost"];

    start [label="for each root,\nin priority order", shape=ellipse];
    nextver [label="take the next-newest\ncandidate version of root"];
    trial [label="pin root == that version\n(plus every already-fixed\nhigher-priority root)\nsolve_feasibility()", fillcolor="#FF655D", fontcolor="white"];
    feasible [label="feasible?", shape=diamond, fillcolor="#F1DB4B"];
    keep [label="fix this version\nfor root"];
    nextroot [label="advance to\nthe next root", shape=ellipse];
    fail [label="unsatisfiable stack:\nno version of root works\nwith higher-priority pins", fillcolor="#FF655D", fontcolor="white"];

    start -> nextver;
    nextver -> trial;
    trial -> feasible;
    feasible -> keep [label="yes"];
    feasible -> nextver [label="no: try the\nnext-oldest version"];
    keep -> nextroot;
    nextver -> fail [label="no versions left", style=dashed];
}
```

Each trial re-solves feasibility (a fresh resolvo SAT call) with the
candidate version pinned as an exact requirement alongside every
higher-priority root's already-fixed version. The first version that keeps
the whole trial feasible is kept; the loop never backtracks past a
higher-priority root once fixed. After every root has a fixed version, one
final solve with all root pins in place produces the lock: non-root,
non-priority packages still prefer newer via resolvo's own
`sort_candidates` heuristic, since nothing forces them to a specific
version.

This priority layer is deliberately **not** a joint, whole-stack optimum: it is a
lexicographic optimum over the declared priority order. That is a stronger
guarantee than plain SAT feasibility, and it is enough to make multi-root
outcomes depend only on the policy (including `root_priority`) and the
candidate set, never on incidental candidate list order or map iteration
order. It is not a claim that the result maximizes some single scalar
objective across every co-selected package simultaneously; a true
multi-objective optimum would need a different (and considerably more
expensive) formulation on top of the same SAT core.

# What this guarantees in practice

- Single-root policies: priority reduces to one root, so this is "newest
  feasible version of the root plus newest feasible everything else":
  the common case, and the fast path.
- Multi-root policies with no shared-dependency conflict: every root gets
  its newest version; the priority order never has to break a tie.
- Multi-root policies **with** a conflict: the declared `root_priority`
  decides, not candidate list order, not `HashMap` iteration, not which
  root happened to be listed first in `roots`.

# The parser approach

# Easyconfigs are Python, but eb-stack does not run Python

An EasyBuild easyconfig (`*.eb`) is, syntactically, a Python source file.
EasyBuild's own framework loads it by executing it and reading the resulting
module namespace. That gives EasyBuild full fidelity (conditionals,
computed values, imports, templating via `%(version)s`-style substitution)
at the cost of needing a Python interpreter and the EasyBuild framework
installed, and of executing arbitrary code from every recipe it reads.

`eb_parse` (`src/eb_parse.rs`) does not run a Python interpreter. It
evaluates easyconfigs as a **restricted Python-like domain-specific language (DSL)** with its own small
recursive-descent parser: string/int/bool/`None` literals, lists, tuples,
dicts, name lookups (including `local_*` variables and the `SYSTEM`
constant), `+` string concatenation, `%` string formatting, and the full
EasyBuild `TEMPLATE_CONSTANTS` table (`SOURCE_TAR_GZ`, `GITHUB_SOURCE`,
`PYPI_SOURCE`, and around fifty others: see `src/eb_template_constants.rs`).
Unmodeled statements (`for`, `def`, `import`, and similar keywords) are
skipped rather than rejected, so a recipe that uses control flow for a field
`eb-stack` does not need still yields every field it does need. One `if` is
read: `if ARCH == '<this machine>'`, with the body parsed as easyconfig
text. `name.append(...)` extends a list or tuple that is already assigned, so
an architecture-specific `dependencies.append` is part of the closure on that
machine. Any other `if` is skipped.

# What gets resolved

`resolve_easyconfig_str` (and its file wrapper, `resolve_easyconfig_file`)
evaluates the whole assignment namespace, then extracts and template-expands:

- `name`, `version`, `versionsuffix`
- `toolchain` (dict form `{'name': ..., 'version': ...}`, tuple form, or the
  bare `SYSTEM` constant)
- `dependencies` and `builddependencies`: 2-, 3-, or 4-element tuples
  (name, version, optional versionsuffix, optional per-dependency
  toolchain override), plus the legacy filename form
  (`'OpenMPI-4.1.6-foss-2025b.eb'`) some easyconfigs still use
- `exts_list`: name/version pairs, string-only entries, and entries with a
  trailing options dict

A bare dependency version (`'4.1.5'`) maps to an **exact** solver requirement
(`==4.1.5`), EasyBuild's own default dependency semantics, while a
version already carrying `=``, `>``, `<``, `>`, `<`, or `!`` is used as-is.

`%(key)s` templates are resolved against a per-recipe template table built
from `name`/`version`/`versionsuffix`/`toolchain` (including derived keys
like `namelower`, `version_major_minor`, `github_account`) plus the static
`TEMPLATE_CONSTANTS` table, applied recursively (bounded) so a constant that
itself expands to another template still resolves. A recipe assignment of
`github_account`, `bitbucket_account`, or `versionprefix` replaces the derived
value. Without one, the forge accounts stay at `namelower` and `versionprefix`
stays unset.

This resolved shape feeds `recipe check`, `stack solve`, and the candidate
universe for `package bump` through
`ResolvedEasyconfig::to_candidate()`. A bump also resolves its source recipe,
materializes an EasyBuild-origin package plan, and asks Resolvo for the target
dependency selection. The targeted emitter then locates the `toolchain` dict,
`version` assignment, checksum entry, and dependency tuples in the original
source text and rewrites only those spans. Unselected content stays intact,
while the selected versions come from the profile lock rather than a separate
text-rewrite decision path. See [architecture](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/architecture.html.md).

# Correctness is checked against EasyBuild's own parser

`fixtures/parser_hardcases/` contains small easyconfigs exercising the
constructs above (template substitution, `local_*` variables, the
`SYSTEM` toolchain, multi-element dependency tuples, `exts_list`) paired
with golden JSON under `fixtures/parser_hardcases/resolved/` produced by
`scripts/resolve_easyconfig_eb.py`, which drives EasyBuild's real
`EasyConfigParser` (requires an EasyBuild install; not run by ~cargo
test`). `cargo test~ asserts the Rust parser's output against those
checked-in goldens: a change to `eb_parse` that diverges from what
EasyBuild itself would produce fails a test.

# Unparseable files are skipped, not fatal

Real easyconfig trees are large (annual EasyBuild checkouts run to five
figures of `.eb` files) and not every file in a checkout parses: some use
constructs outside the restricted DSL (inline `if`/`for`, multi-statement
`configopts` built from several `+=` lines with embedded control flow,
computed values). `parse_easyconfig_tree` walks the whole directory and
records each unparseable file in `ParseTreeResult::skipped` with its error;
it does not abort the walk on the first bad file. `ParseTreeResult::coverage()`
reports the parsed fraction. Tree-consuming commands such as `recipe check`,
`stack solve`, and `package bump --easyconfigs` surface coverage and sample
skips, so "not in the candidate universe" and "does not exist" stay
distinguishable to the operator reading the output.

Coverage against a real, unfiltered `easybuilders/easybuild-easyconfigs`
checkout (tens of thousands of files, every toolchain generation from
`2021a` onward) stays above 90%: see
[reproduction fidelity and limitations](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/fidelity.html.md) for the exact
number and what the remaining unparsed files look like.

# Why targeted evaluation instead of the alternatives

Two more general options exist and were deliberately not taken:

- **Evaluate the file with a Python interpreter**, optionally driving
  EasyBuild's own `EasyConfig` class for full parity with what EasyBuild
  itself would parse. This gives ground-truth fidelity, including
  computed and templated fields no restricted evaluator will ever handle,
  at the cost of pulling a Python runtime (and, for true parity, an
  EasyBuild install) into a Rust CLI's dependency chain, and of executing
  recipe code `eb-stack` did not author.
- **A full Parsing Expression Grammar (PEG) or hand-written grammar** for the easyconfig DSL (the
  `pest`/`chumsky`/`nom`/`lalrpop` family). This stays native and
  dependency-free like the current approach, but is strictly more
  implementation effort to track EasyBuild's own syntax evolution, for a
  grammar that still would not evaluate control flow or computed values
  any more than the current restricted evaluator does.

The restricted recursive-descent evaluator is a deliberate middle ground:
real assignment/expression evaluation (not a text-scraping regex layer) for
every construct the solver and the emit path need, without a Python
runtime and without evaluating arbitrary code. It does not (and is not
meant to) handle a field whose value depends on control flow, a function
call, or an import: those recipes fail that one field's extraction and
the file is skipped, not miscounted as present with a wrong value.

# Version comparison is EasyBuild-shaped, not semver

`src/version.rs` tokenizes a version string into an ordered run of numeric
and alphabetic parts and compares position by position: numeric parts
compare numerically, alphabetic parts compare lexicographically, and a
trailing alphabetic part with nothing on the other side sorts as a
pre-release (`2025a < 2025b`, `1.0rc1 < 1.0`). This matches how EasyBuild
toolchain generations (`2025a`, `2025b`) and application pre-releases
actually sort, which semver's `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` model does not directly
express.

# Reproduction fidelity and limitations

`eb-stack` separates deterministic package planning from empirical build
evidence. This page states what the checked-in regression suites prove and
where an operator must rely on residuals or a target campaign instead of a
compatibility assumption.

# Evidence boundaries

| Evidence | What it proves | What it does not prove |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Parser and package fixtures | Input facts survive normalization into the package plan and planned Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) | The selected package compiles |
| Resolvo profile lock | One dependency selection satisfies the declared constraints, pins, exclusions, and EasyBuild hierarchy | The selected versions are ABI-compatible in a real build |
| Emitted-recipe regression | The rendered `.eb` text and bundle layout match a frozen expected result | Upstream source bytes, patches, compilers, tests, or sanity succeed |
| Campaign state | EasyBuild and declared verification commands ran on one named target | The same recipe builds on a different target or runtime ABI |

The claim ladder follows these boundaries: planning may establish **resolves**;
only a target campaign may establish **builds** and **binary-verified**.
New packages enter this boundary through `eb-stack package plan`; existing
recipes use `eb-stack package bump`; whole-stack selection uses
`eb-stack stack solve`.

# Frozen maintainer-bump matrix

`tests/reproduce_real_prs.rs` contains 18 library and CLI regressions over six
real `foss-2023b` to `foss-2024a` recipe pairs:

- GROMACS 2024.4;
- ScaFaCoS 1.0.4;
- MDTraj 1.10.3;
- Fiona 1.10.1;
- PuLP 2.8.0;
- numba 0.60.0.

The zero-hand-fed cases give `package bump` only the source recipe, target
toolchain generation, and frozen EasyBuild universe. Resolvo selects the
hierarchy-compatible dependency identities. ScaFaCoS, MDTraj, Fiona, PuLP,
and numba reproduce the frozen target content. GROMACS matches after removing
the one `pybind11` dependency added by the maintainer; the regression also
asserts that `eb-stack` does not invent that source-absent dependency.

`tests/bump_emit.rs` separately checks canonical bundle paths, deterministic
repeat runs, explicit version/checksum inputs, hierarchy-aware selection, and
parity between the library and `eb-stack package bump` CLI paths.

Run the public regression:

```bash
cargo test --locked \
  --test reproduce_real_prs \
  --test bump_emit \
  -- --nocapture
```

This is a fixed regression matrix, not a success-rate estimate for arbitrary
EasyBuild recipes.

# Foreign-package and profile evidence

The conda-forge eOn and Spack QMCPACK fixtures exercise a different boundary:

- static recipe ingestion with source spans and provenance;
- conda selectors and Spack conditions, variants, conflicts, and requirements;
- canonical package plans and CycloneDX 1.5 planned SBOMs;
- per-profile Resolvo locks;
- one conventional recipe per independently loadable variant;
- stack-pin fallback and candidate exclusions;
- packaging gates against frozen overlays and, when configured, a real robot.

Run those deterministic suites:

```bash
cargo test --locked \
  --test foreign_ingest \
  --test foreign_conditions \
  --test profile_emission \
  --test eon_core_rgpot \
  --test eon_foss_2026_1 \
  --test qmcpack_foss_2026_1 \
  --test eon_packaging \
  -- --nocapture
```

These tests establish parser, solver, and emitter behavior. They do not replace
`campaign run` on the selected EasyBuild target.

# Cross-source LAMMPS control

LAMMPS is a cross-source control for the generic foreign-package path. The
conda-forge and Spack fixtures describe the same upstream product through
different recipe languages. The conda fixture exercises multiple sources,
feedstock patches, selectors, and build/output dependency roles; the Spack
fixture exercises version URL generation, resources, variants, conflicts, and
conditional dependencies. Static Spack patch directives use the same artifact
model as conda patches, including checksum and applicability; version-excluded
patches do not leak into the selected build manifest.

Both inputs pass through the same parser-neutral package plan, selector
materialization, Resolvo selection, CycloneDX emission, closure expansion, and
EasyBuild renderer used by other packages. Production parser code does not
dispatch on the LAMMPS package name. `examples/packages/lammps.toml` is public,
authored EasyBuild product policy: it records easyblock parameters, package
features, verification commands, and reviewed patches in data rather than
embedding those decisions in a parser.

The generated conda closure includes source-only dependencies such as `mlip`
and `n2p2` when their Linux selectors apply. Feedstock patches survive package
policy through `patches_mode = "merge"`, and same-filename policy entries may
replace their metadata without duplicating an artifact. Recipe checks over the
root and generated companions establish the **resolves** rung. They deliberately
make no **builds** or **binary-verified** claim without a target campaign.

Run the cross-source parser and profile regressions:

```bash
cargo test --locked \
  --test foreign_ingest \
  --test foreign_conditions \
  --test package_config \
  --test profile_emission \
  -- --nocapture
```

# Real-tree parser scale

`tests/real_tree_scale.rs` walks an unfiltered EasyBuild checkout when
`EB_EASYCONFIGS` points at one. `scripts/fetch-upstream-trees.sh` writes that
variable into `env.sh`. The test requires more than 1,000 recipes, asserts at
least 90% coverage of the restricted domain-specific language (DSL), and exercises canonical GROMACS, numba, and
nglview bumps against that live candidate universe:

```bash
EB_EASYCONFIGS="$EB_EASYCONFIGS" \
  cargo test --locked --test real_tree_scale -- --nocapture
```

Files outside the restricted EasyBuild DSL are reported as skipped paths with
parse errors; one file does not abort the tree walk. See
[the parser approach](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/parser-approach.html.md) for the supported expression
model.

# Scoring a bump against a merged PR

The reproduction grind scores an emitted bump against the file an
EasyBuild maintainer actually merged. `eb_stack::score_reproduction`
places each file on one of three rungs:

| Score | Means |
| --- | --- |
| `EXACT` | The same bytes as the merged file. |
| `SEMANTIC` | Differs only in ways that cannot change the build. |
| `MATERIAL` | A real difference in what would be built. |

The reproduction rungs are what `eb-stack repro summary --scores DIR`
prints from the per-case JSON the suite writes. `--json` prints the records. `--ratchet FILE`
compares each case's allowance with the committed counts and exits
nonzero on a disagreement. The columns are case, pull request, score,
allowance (hand-added lines still forgiven), and residual diff lines.

Two rungs used on the scoreboard have no place in this function, because
they are decided before any comparison: `ERROR` (no file was produced)
and `excluded` (the file was never a scoreable bump, such as a toolchain
meta-recipe or a backfill). An exclusion is recorded with its reason
rather than dropped from the denominator.

`EXACT` stays raw equality. Only the `SEMANTIC` against `MATERIAL` line
is drawn on normalized text, by `eb_stack::normalize_for_scoring`, which
removes comment-only lines, comment tails, trailing whitespace, and runs
of blank lines. String content survives verbatim: a triple-quoted
`description` carries its blank lines, its indentation, and any `#` it
contains into the built module, so normalizing inside one would call two
different module descriptions equivalent.

The distinction is not academic. Scoring PR #25009 (LLVM v21.1.8, merge
`3e86bdac`) found three divergences in one file: a stale commented-out
`toolchainopts` entry the bump preserved and the merge deleted, one
blank-line difference, and a patch set the merge narrowed. A raw text
diff reports all three as one `MATERIAL` verdict, which flattens exactly
the distinction the ladder exists to make; the first two cannot change
what gets built, and the third builds different sources.

`eb_stack::compare_reproduction` returns the score together with the raw
line diff, never the normalized one. A forgiving verdict is only
auditable if the reader can see the difference it forgave.

Normalization that changed a recipe's meaning would not fail loudly.
It would instead make two files that build different things score
`SEMANTIC`. So `tests/repro_scoring.rs` asserts the property directly:
normalizing a recipe leaves the resolved easyconfig identical, over the
checked-in fixtures always and over the robot tree when one is present.

```bash
EB_EASYCONFIGS="$EB_EASYCONFIGS" \
  EB_REQUIRE_EASYCONFIGS=1 \
  cargo test --locked --test repro_scoring -- --nocapture
```

# Limits that remain explicit

- **Static foreign parsing:** dynamic Python, Jinja, helper calls, or imported
  logic that cannot be proven from source becomes a residual. The parser does
  not execute conda-forge or Spack recipe code. Informational parser notes do
  not become residuals merely because their text describes dynamic source
  logic; residual classification is typed at the parser boundary.
- **Candidate-universe scope:** Resolvo can select only identities present in
  the supplied robot trees. Pass upstream first and overlays afterward so the
  reviewed site identity wins.
- **Stack policy:** a `preferred` pin may fall back to another jointly feasible
  candidate and records that outcome. A `locked` pin makes incompatibility
  unsatisfiable. Neither mode claims that the candidate builds.
- **Application-version changes:** source URLs and checksums cannot be inferred
  from the old recipe. Supply `--source-checksum`, or `--fetch-checksums` to
  download the artifact the recipe's `source_urls` name and hash those bytes.
  Patches and source-layout changes remain visible residual work.
- **Maintainer additions:** a source recipe cannot reveal a dependency, patch,
  easyblock change, or configuration rule introduced only in the target
  recipe. Add that authored package knowledge, re-plan, and retain it in the
  bundle.
- **Planned SBOM scope:** the CycloneDX document describes requested components
  and selections. It is not an installed-files inventory or binary provenance
  attestation.
- **Target specificity:** a build on one host/container/toolchain ABI does not
  generalize to another. Keep the target name and routed command in campaign
  evidence.

Unresolved dependencies and unsatisfiable locked pins fail the planning
command. Build-compatible claims that fail configure, compile, link, test,
install, or sanity become typed campaign findings. Hermes owns the full repair
loop; OMP workers claim findings, repair the evidence-supported layer, record
the resolution, and rerun the campaign.

  for the batch workflow and claim ladder.

  `package bump` inputs and bundle.
- [Campaign state and typed findings](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/../reference/campaigns.html.md) for
  empirical build classification and ownership.
- [Tutorial](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/../tutorial.html.md) for conda-forge eOn plus the QMCPACK
  profile variant.

# From one easystack line to a build set

`eb-stack pr-overlap` turns each easystack line a pull request adds into the
modules that line would build on the installed stack. This page follows open
European Environment for Scientific Software Installations (EESSI) software-layer pull requests 1728 and 1787 for 2026.06, against
`/cvmfs/software.eessi.io` `x86_64/amd/zen4`, using the easyconfigs that come
with EasyBuild 5.4.0. The zen4 run loaded `EESSI-extend` and passed that
module's `EASYBUILD_FILTER_DEPS`, the `modules/all` tree, and the EasyBuild
5.4.0 easyblocks package. The command writes records. It does not build.

The commands that produce the same files are in
[find shared builds across open pull requests](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/../howto/pr-overlap.html.md).
The record fields are in [output formats](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/../reference/formats.html.md).

# One line

Pull request 1759 adds one line to
`easystacks/software.eessi.io/2026.06/eessi-2026.06-eb-5.4.0-2026.1.yml`.
A diff of that easystack, base against head, adds:

```text
+  - lfbf-2026.1.eb
```

The dry run below used an easystack that contains only that line.

# Closure

`lfbf-2026.1.eb` is a toolchain recipe. The fields the closure reads are:

```text
toolchain = SYSTEM

local_llvmver = '21.1.8'

dependencies = [
    ('llvm-compilers', local_llvmver),
    ('FlexiBLAS', '3.5.0', '', ('llvm-compilers', local_llvmver)),
    ('FFTW', '3.3.10', '', ('llvm-compilers', local_llvmver)),
]
```

The recipe assigns no `builddependencies`. An installed module is a leaf, so
the walk records these three dependencies and does not open them. The module
names in the record are:

```text
lfbf/2026.1                                          to build
├── llvm-compilers/21.1.8                            installed
├── FlexiBLAS/3.5.0-llvm-compilers-21.1.8            installed
│     toolchain: llvm-compilers/21.1.8
└── FFTW/3.3.10-llvm-compilers-21.1.8                installed
      toolchain: llvm-compilers/21.1.8
```

`lfbf` itself uses the system toolchain, which is omitted from the module
name. `FlexiBLAS` and `FFTW` pin `llvm-compilers` 21.1.8, which is the
installed `llvm-compilers/21.1.8` module.

# The record

`prs/1759.toml` from the zen4 run
(`generated_at = "2026-10-19T14:07:20Z"`):

```text
# Generated by `eb-stack pr-overlap`. Data only: the branch holding this file is
# regenerated on every run and must never be merged.

schema_version = 1
pr = 1759
head_sha = "d8bf804c46ebf467355123c8b103bafe4a545b63"
title = "{2026.06}[2026.1] lfbf-2026.1"
generated_at = "2026-10-19T14:07:20Z"
eessi_version = "2026.06"
installed_source = "x86_64/amd/zen4"
easystack_files = ["easystacks/software.eessi.io/2026.06/eessi-2026.06-eb-5.4.0-2026.1.yml"]
to_build = [
  "lfbf/2026.1",
]
already_installed = ["FFTW/3.3.10-llvm-compilers-21.1.8", "FlexiBLAS/3.5.0-llvm-compilers-21.1.8", "llvm-compilers/21.1.8"]
unresolved = []

[[entries]]
easystack = "easystacks/software.eessi.io/2026.06/eessi-2026.06-eb-5.4.0-2026.1.yml"
easyconfig = "lfbf-2026.1.eb"
eb_version = "5.4.0"
```

`to_build` is the one module the pull request would build.
`already_installed` is the three leaves. `unresolved` is empty.

One line is `[ ]`, and it is `lfbf/2026.1`, the only `to_build` entry.
`llvm-compilers/21.1.8`, `FlexiBLAS/3.5.0-llvm-compilers-21.1.8`, and
`FFTW/3.3.10-llvm-compilers-21.1.8` are `[x]`, matching `already_installed`.
The other 40 `[x]` lines are dependencies of those installed modules.
The closure stops at an installed module, so they are not in the record.

# Two pull requests, one shared module

Pull request 1728 adds one line to the same easystack:

```text
+  - PLUMED-2.10.0-foss-2026.1.eb
```

Pull request 1787 adds:

```text
+  - LAMMPS-30Sep2026-foss-2026.1-kokkos.eb:
+      options:
+        # See https://github.com/easybuilders/easybuild-easyblocks/pull/4258
+        include-easyblocks-from-commit: c4dd34fe568e8b98bf6cf70e97a92c04266f1ef4
+        # See https://github.com/easybuilders/easybuild-easyconfigs/pull/27161
+        from-commit: 4aa3da2770dccf4ab7dba9c3fabbdbb84b6025f4
```

`LAMMPS-30Sep2026-foss-2026.1-kokkos.eb` at that `from-commit` has
`toolchain = {'name': 'foss', 'version': '2026.1'}` and, in `dependencies`,
`('PLUMED', '2.10.0')`. `PLUMED-2.10.0-foss-2026.1.eb` uses the same
toolchain. `PLUMED/2.10.0-foss-2026.1` is not on the zen4 installed list, so
both records put it in `to_build`. 1728 lists it because the pull request
adds it. 1787 lists it because the closure of LAMMPS needs it. Pull request
1777 adds the same `PLUMED-2.10.0-foss-2026.1.eb` line, so its record lists
the module too.

The zen4 run's filter list, from `module load EESSI-extend`:

```text
ZEN4_FILTER=binutils,bzip2,DBus,flex,gettext,gperf,help2man,intltool,libreadline,makeinfo,ncurses,NVPL,ParMETIS,util-linux,XZ,zlib
prs=39 records=18 shared_modules=9 skipped_easyconfigs=0 out=/tmp/out-fix
```

A name on that list is dropped before the walk, and the modules reachable
only through it are never opened. `prs/1728.toml` therefore has a single
`to_build` line:

```text
# Generated by `eb-stack pr-overlap`. Data only: the branch holding this file is
# regenerated on every run and must never be merged.

schema_version = 1
pr = 1728
head_sha = "252edc963ef08b209cd73330149f2c345a2536be"
title = "{2026.06}[2026.1] PLUMED-2.10.0"

eessi_version = "2026.06"

easystack_files = ["easystacks/software.eessi.io/2026.06/eessi-2026.06-eb-5.4.0-2026.1.yml"]
to_build = [
  "PLUMED/2.10.0-foss-2026.1",
]
already_installed = ["Boost/1.90.0-GCCcore-15.2.0", "Cython/3.2.4-GCCcore-15.2.0", "GSL/2.8-GCC-15.2.0", "Python/3.14.2-GCCcore-15.2.0", "SciPy-bundle/2026.05-gfbf-2026.1", "foss/2026.1", "xxd/9.2.0612-GCCcore-15.2.0"]
unresolved = []
```


`to_build` is one sorted line per module, so a duplicate line is a module
both pull requests would build. This checkout records that check on
`tests/pr_overlap_layer`, pull requests 1585 and 1728:

```bash
eb-stack pr-overlap --pr tests/pr_overlap_layer/prs.json \
  --easyconfigs tests/pr_overlap_layer \
  --installed tests/pr_overlap_layer/installed.txt \
  --installed-label none \
  --generated-at 2026-10-24T00:00:00Z \
  --repo-url https://github.com/EESSI/software-layer \
  --eessi-version 2026.06 \
  --out-dir /tmp/pr-overlap-recorded
awk '/^to_build = \[\]/{next} /^to_build = \[/{f=1; next} f && /^\]/{f=0; next} f' \
  /tmp/pr-overlap-recorded/prs/*.toml | sort | uniq -d
```

```text
 * [ ] /cvmfs/software.eessi.io/versions/2026.06/software/linux/x86_64/amd/zen4/software/EasyBuild/5.4.0/easybuild/easyconfigs/m/MPC/MPC-1.4.1-GCCcore-15.2.0.eb (module: MPC/1.4.1-GCCcore-15.2.0)

```

While `PLUMED/2.10.0-foss-2026.1` is in more than one `to_build`, each of
those pull requests would compile PLUMED and install it. The build that
finishes second overwrites the binary the first build installed. The two
builds can use different hooks, so the copy that remains can be the second
build's binary.

# Merge order and knock-on

1. Edge A -> B when a module in B's `to_build` is an easystack entry A adds
   (A asks for it by name; B only reaches it). Edges both ways form a cycle.
2. Among pull requests with no remaining incoming edge, pick the one whose
   residual build set is smallest, then the lowest pull request number.
3. After picking, add its residual builds to the installed set and recompute
   residuals for the rest. `saves` is that difference.
4. A strongly connected component is reported in `cycles`. Edges inside it
   are dropped, and rule 2 orders its pull requests with every other pull
   request that has no remaining incoming edge.

The module an entry asks for is the easyconfig filename with the package
name and the rest split by `/`, the same `name/version[-toolchain]versionsuffix`
string `to_build` uses. `Lib-1.0-GCCcore-15.2.0.eb` asks for
`Lib/1.0-GCCcore-15.2.0`.

`--merged` numbers are not steps. Their `to_build` modules count as
installed before rule 2 runs. A number that is not in the `--pr` input is
an error, and the message names that number.

`--impact N` answers a narrower question than the sequence. It treats only
N's `to_build` as newly installed, and it does not walk the earlier steps
of the order. Another pull request is listed when its `to_build` shrinks
by a module N also builds, or when a depends-on edge from N resolves: N
asks for the module by name, and the other only reaches it. Both asking
for the module is not an edge, the same rule as step 1. On the freetype
fixture, merging 11 shrinks 12 and 13 by freetype and libpng, and the
freetype edge resolves for 12 only. 13 asks for freetype itself. A number
that is not in the input is an error, and the message names that number.

For each easystack path changed by 2 or more pull requests, the insertion
point is the 0-based index of the base line before the first added line,
from a line longest common subsequence (LCS) of base and head. The point is -1 when the added lines
start at the top of the file. The same point is `same-insertion`. Identical
added lines are `same-entry`. The record keeps that base and head text, or
the blob ids, on `revisions`, and the merge order reads the collisions from
the record.

# What an in-place patch forces a rebuild of

The patch keeps the easyconfig filename and the version. ~eb-stack
rebuild-set~ closes the deployed easystacks and walks backward from each
patched easyconfig through the installed modules. The closure is everything
that depends on the patched module within its toolchain generation. An
unpinned dependency is resolved inside the dependent's own generation, so
a module built with another generation is not a row.

The walk starts from the easyconfig graph. `--prefix` and `--check-static`
then read the installed files. The commands are in
[what an in-place patch forces the European Environment for Scientific Software Installations (EESSI) to rebuild](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/../howto/rebuild-set.html.md).
The output fields are in [output formats](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/../reference/formats.html.md).

# Three classes

- `no-rebuild`. Some path from the patched module is made of runtime
  dependencies. The dependent links the patched package as a shared
  library. Replacing that library does not require a rebuild.
- `review`. Every path uses a builddependency. The dependent may have
  linked the package statically or embedded it. The graph cannot say
  which, and the reason says so.
- `must-rebuild`. The row is the patched easyconfig, or a bundle whose
  `exts_list` names that package and version. The extension is installed
  as part of the bundle.

The strongest class wins: must-rebuild, then review, then no-rebuild. A
runtime path beats a builddependency path, so a module listed in both
`dependencies` and `builddependencies` is no-rebuild.

An extension makes that bundle must-rebuild. It does not force the same
class on modules that depend on the bundle. Those modules are classified
by their own edges. A runtime dependency on the bundle is no-rebuild, and
the reason names the bundle.

A toolchain edge is indexed and not classified. Patching a compiler is
outside these three classes.

A review dependent is reported once. The changed column lists every
patched easyconfig that put it there. When `--prefix` found static
archives, the reason names them. The other classes stay one row per edge.

# Installed archives

`--prefix` is the installed prefix of EESSI. The install directory of
`Name/version` is `software/Name/version`. A static archive is a `*.a`
file directly under a `lib*` directory there.

A patched module whose directory exists and contains no such file cannot
have been linked statically. A builddependency-only dependent of that
module is no-rebuild, and the reason is `no static archive installed`.
Archives that are there keep the row in review, and the reason names
them. A missing install directory is a note. The row stays in review. A
prefix with no `software` directory is an error.

# Defined symbols

`--check-static` is off unless it is passed, and it needs `--prefix`. It
reads defined dynamic symbols of each remaining review dependent and
compares them with the exports of the patched libraries that put the row
in review. The exports come from `lib**/**.so` and `lib**/**.so.*`, skipping
symlinks. When that set is empty, they come from the global and weak
defined symbols in the `*.a` members. Version suffixes (`@@VERS` and
`@VERS`) are stripped before the comparison.

A hit means the dependent defines an export of the patched library, which
is what a static link copies in. The row becomes must-rebuild, and the
reason names the file and the symbols. No hit, and a readable export set,
is no-rebuild. An empty export set stays in review. A missing install
directory of the dependent is a note, and the row stays in review.

The scan can go wrong. It sees dynamic symbols only, so a hidden, local,
or inlined static link is a false no-rebuild. A short name shared with
another library is a false must-rebuild. Scripts, bytecode, and libraries
opened with dlopen are invisible. A static archive shows that a static
link was possible, not that it happened.

# What counts as installed

The reverse walk visits installed modules only. It does not continue
through a module that is not installed, so a dependent that is reachable
only through an uninstalled intermediate is left out. The patched
easyconfig itself is must-rebuild when it is in the deployed graph, even
when that module is not installed.

`--filter-deps` drops `dependencies` and `builddependencies` tuples before
the walk. It leaves `exts_list` in place. A filtered package that a bundle
includes as an extension still marks that bundle must-rebuild.

A missing easyblock class is a note. The module stays in the set, because
it is already installed. A `from-commit` whose tree was not passed is a
note, and the release tree is used for that pin.

# Example

Patch `zlib-1.3.1-GCCcore-15.2.0.eb`. `libpng` depends on zlib, so libpng
is no-rebuild. `Graphviz` depends on libpng, so Graphviz is no-rebuild
through libpng. `CMake` lists zlib only as a builddependency, so CMake is
review. A bundle whose `exts_list` names zlib 1.3.1 is must-rebuild. An
application that depends on that bundle at runtime is no-rebuild.

The rebuild easystack contains zlib and the bundle, each with
`rebuild: true`. It does not contain libpng.

With `--prefix`, the CMake row stays in review only when the installed
zlib provides a static archive, and the reason names that archive. With
`--check-static`, CMake is must-rebuild when one of its installed Executable and Linkable Format (ELF)
files defines an export of that archive, and no-rebuild when none of
them does.

# Dependency closure

A dependency closure lists every module one change reaches. The change
may be an easyconfig, an easyblock, or one bundled component. A software
bill of materials (SBOM) records the components and the edges. The record
is planned: the recipes supply it before anything is installed.

An easyconfig author reads the closure of one recipe bump. A reviewer
compares pull requests that share a file or a module. An easyblock author
lists the recipes that name a changed class. A framework author lists
those recipes. Triage lists the installed modules that carry one component
from a Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entry. A software-layer
maintainer lists the pull requests that would build one module. A site
maintainer lists the installed modules an upstream pull request changes.
The annual toolchain bump is the generation step in the first section. A
security or compliance reader consumes the CycloneDX document. A
conda-forge porter reads the planned SBOM from `package inspect`. A Spack
porter reads that document too.

The runs below use recorded slices of upstream trees.
`tests/sbom_recorded/cbc`, `tests/sbom_recorded/gromacs`,
`tests/sbom_recorded/quarto`, and `tests/sbom_recorded/rebuild` are byte
copies of easybuild-easyconfigs `develop` at
`981d2123dddccca9ce0b15f9eb2643e872332f5e`, the commit
`scripts/fetch-upstream-trees.sh` creates a checkout of. The easyconfigs under
`tests/pr_overlap_layer` are the same kind of copy. `prs.json` there is
the recorded pull-request file for software-layer pull requests 1585 and 1728.
`tests/sbom_recorded/easyblock` is a byte copy of the v5.4.1 easyblocks,
framework, and easyconfigs tags that script pins.
`tests/sbom_recorded/foreign` is the conda-forge zlib feedstock recipe at
`e34000ac354055f133215d211048bc3289afe5f4` and the Spack zlib `package.py`
at `a19611deab3c33e3b2855b8379e8ddee12ef843a`. Each directory keeps the
upstream licence file. `tests/pr_overlap_easyconfigs_open` is the recorded
open easybuild-easyconfigs pull requests.
`tests/component_reach_recorded` is the cURL and git slice from the same
develop commit. The runs write under `/tmp/sbom-demo`.

```bash
eb-stack --version
```

```text
eb-stack 0.3.0
```

The how-tos name the flags for each command:
[pull-request overlap](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/../howto/pr-overlap.html.md),
[an in-place patch](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/../howto/rebuild-set.html.md),
[a named component](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/../howto/component-reach.html.md),
[an easyblock change](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/../howto/easyblock-reach.html.md), and
[a recipe bump](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/../howto/bump-recipe.html.md). Output fields are in
[output formats](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/../reference/formats.html.md).

# The annual toolchain bump

A generation maintainer asks which packages change version together.
The recorded step is foss-2025a to foss-2025b for Cbc. The slice has the
foss-2025b closure of `Cbc-2.10.12` and the foss-2025a counterparts of
Cbc, Cgl, Clp, and MUMPS. `stack solve --sbom-out` writes a CycloneDX 1.5
document for the selection. `stack sbom --lock` writes the same document
later, from the lock. Both commands read edges and checksums from the
easyconfigs the lock names. A runtime dependency that is also selected is
a `dependsOn` edge. A builddependency is the component property
`eb_stack:buildDependsOn`. The document does not draw an edge from every
package to every other package.

`--build-list-out` writes the easyconfigs to build.
`--jenkins-roots-only` writes one Jenkins line for the policy root and
leaves the dependencies to `eb --robot`.

```bash
eb-stack stack solve \
  --easyconfigs tests/sbom_recorded/cbc \
  --baseline-easyconfigs tests/sbom_recorded/cbc \
  --toolchain foss/2025b \
  --root Cbc \
  --lock-out /tmp/sbom-demo/stack.lock.json \
  --sbom-out /tmp/sbom-demo/stack.cdx.json \
  --stack-diff-out /tmp/sbom-demo/stack.diff.md \
  --build-list-out /tmp/sbom-demo/build.list \
  --jenkins-build-list-out /tmp/sbom-demo/jenkins.list \
  --jenkins-roots-only
```

```text
lock=/tmp/sbom-demo/stack.lock.json packages=58
```

```bash
cat /tmp/sbom-demo/build.list
```

# A CycloneDX consumer

A scanner identifies these components by package URL. The type is
`pkg:generic`. The document carries no Common Platform Enumeration (CPE)
identity. `compositions[0].aggregate` is `complete` when the solve named
every dependency.

```bash
echo aggregate=$(jq -r '.compositions[0].aggregate' /tmp/sbom-demo/stack.cdx.json)
echo purl=$(jq -r '.components[] | select(.name=="Cbc") | .purl' /tmp/sbom-demo/stack.cdx.json)
echo cpe=$(jq -r '[.components[] | .cpe // empty] | length' /tmp/sbom-demo/stack.cdx.json)
```

```text
aggregate=complete
purl=pkg:generic/Cbc@2.10.12?toolchain=foss-2025b
cpe=0
```

# A conda-forge or Spack porter

`package inspect` writes the planned SBOM for one foreign recipe. The
conda-forge file is `recipe/meta.yaml` from `conda-forge/zlib-feedstock`
at `e34000ac354055f133215d211048bc3289afe5f4`. The package name in that
recipe is `zlib-split` and the version is 1.3.2. The Spack file is
`package.py` from `spack/spack-packages` at
`a19611deab3c33e3b2855b8379e8ddee12ef843a`. The licence texts sit next to
the recipes. A build-only dependency is `eb_stack:buildDependsOn`. It is
absent from `dependsOn`. The package-plan document kind stays
`eb-stack:document-kind`, value `canonical-package-plan`.

```bash
eb-stack package inspect \

  --out-dir /tmp/sbom-demo/conda
```

# A checksum dict when the version changes

The hash in that SBOM has to name the artifact the new version will fetch.
`quarto-1.8.26.eb` on develop uses the SYSTEM toolchain. `local_archs`
sends `aarch64` to `arm64` and `x86_64` to `amd64`. `sources` indexes that
map with `ARCH`. The checksum dict has an `amd64` key and an `arm64` key.
A version bump passes one digest on `--source-checksum`.

```bash
eb-stack package bump \
  --source tests/sbom_recorded/quarto/easybuild/easyconfigs/q/quarto/quarto-1.8.26.eb \
  --toolchain system \
  --version 1.8.27 \
  --source-checksum dddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddd \
  --easyconfigs tests/sbom_recorded/quarto \
  --out-dir /tmp/sbom-demo/ck/out
```

```text
manifest=/tmp/sbom-demo/ck/out/package.plan.json
sbom=/tmp/sbom-demo/ck/out/package.sbom.cdx.json
lock=/tmp/sbom-demo/ck/out/locks/default.lock.json
easyconfig=/tmp/sbom-demo/ck/out/easyconfigs/q/quarto/quarto-1.8.27.eb
```

```bash
cat /tmp/sbom-demo/ck/out/easyconfigs/q/quarto/quarto-1.8.27.eb
```

```text
easyblock = 'Tarball'

name = 'quarto'
version = '1.8.27'

homepage = 'https://quarto.org/'
description = '''
    An open-source scientific and technical publishing system.
'''

toolchain = SYSTEM

source_urls = ['https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/releases/download/v%(version)s/']
local_archs = {'aarch64': 'arm64', 'x86_64': 'amd64'}
sources = ['quarto-%%(version)s-linux-%s.tar.gz' % local_archs[ARCH]]

checksums = [{
    'quarto-%(version)s-linux-amd64.tar.gz': 'dddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddd',
    'quarto-%(version)s-linux-arm64.tar.gz': '',
}]

modextrapaths = {'PATH': ''}

sanity_check_paths = {
    'files': ['bin/quarto'],
    'dirs': []
}

sanity_check_commands = ["quarto check"]

moduleclass = 'devel'
```

The expression key is renamed to 1.8.27 and receives the digest from
`--source-checksum`. The arm64 key is renamed and left empty. The easyblock
stays `Tarball`. The SBOM root hash is the digest that was passed in.

```bash
jq -r '.metadata.component.hashes[0] | "\(.alg) \(.content)"' /tmp/sbom-demo/ck/out/package.sbom.cdx.json
```

```text
SHA-256 dddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddddd
```

```bash
jq '.components | length' /tmp/sbom-demo/ck/out/package.sbom.cdx.json
```

```text
1
```

`recipe lint` reports the doubled percent sign that the recipe uses so a
later `%` expansion leaves one percent. `recipe check` resolves the
metadata and counts both checksum slots.

```bash
eb-stack recipe lint /tmp/sbom-demo/ck/out/easyconfigs/q/quarto/quarto-1.8.27.eb | jq -c '{clean, error_free, codes: [.style[].code]}'
```

```text
{"clean":true,"error_free":true,"codes":["EB_FMT_PERCENT"]}
```

```bash
eb-stack recipe check \
  --recipe /tmp/sbom-demo/ck/out/easyconfigs/q/quarto/quarto-1.8.27.eb \
  --easyconfigs tests/sbom_recorded/quarto
```

```text
    "name": "system",

recipe resolves
```

# Pull requests

A software-layer maintainer wants the shared modules. The recorded pair is
pull requests 1585 and 1728 on `EESSI/software-layer` at
`b2c10c7278f8b741f4053ddb2907dc4d062063d1`. Both change
`easystacks/software.eessi.io/2026.06/eessi-2026.06-eb-5.4.0-2026.1.yml`.
1585 adds `SciPy-bundle-2026.05-gfbf-2026.1.eb`. 1728 adds
`PLUMED-2.10.0-foss-2026.1.eb`, and that recipe depends on SciPy-bundle
2026.05. The JSON in `tests/pr_overlap_layer/prs.json` is the base and
head text of that easystack for each pull request. The easyconfigs tree
is the 109 modules the two closures reach, copied from
develop `981d2123dddccca9ce0b15f9eb2643e872332f5e`. The installed list is a
comment, because this checkout has no mounted prefix. `--installed` is
still required for the software-layer kind.
`prs/<N>.toml` is the build set for pull request N. `overlap.toml` and
`overlap.md` are the intersection.

The 1585/1728 pair is a replay of a recorded state. Pull request 1585
merged on 2026-09-04. The recorded base of 1728 already lists
`SciPy-bundle-2026.05-gfbf-2026.1.eb`. The two used different bases.
The command replays 1728's easystack against an empty `installed.txt`,
which is why the pair shares 91 modules.

To run it on live pull requests, clone `EESSI/software-layer` and write
one JSON file per open pull request with
`examples/eessi-pr-overlap/fetch-prs.sh`. Pass those files as repeated
`--pr` arguments, and pass the prefix's installed module list as
`--installed`. [The how-to](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/../howto/pr-overlap.html.md) gives the
commands under "Run it on a mounted stack".

The software-layer kind keeps an easystack whose path contains
`--eessi-version`. The default is 2026.06. The easyconfigs kind ignores
the flag.

```bash
eb-stack pr-overlap \
  --pr tests/pr_overlap_layer/prs.json \
  --easyconfigs tests/pr_overlap_layer \
  --installed tests/pr_overlap_layer/installed.txt \
  --installed-label none \
  --generated-at 2026-10-24T00:00:00Z \
  --repo-url https://github.com/EESSI/software-layer \
  --eessi-version 2026.06 \
  --out-dir /tmp/sbom-demo/pr/out
```

```text
prs=2 records=2 shared_modules=91 skipped_easyconfigs=0 out=/tmp/sbom-demo/pr/out
```

```bash
sed -n '1,8p' /tmp/sbom-demo/pr/out/prs/1585.toml
```

```text
# Generated by `eb-stack pr-overlap`. Data only: the branch holding this file is
# regenerated on every run and must never be merged.

schema_version = 1
pr = 1585
head_sha = "5abcffa10e4d63a6494f51340474a2f95502adf2"
title = "Merge pull request #1585 from bedroge/2026.1_scipy_bundle"
generated_at = "2026-10-24T00:00:00Z"
```

The generated-file header comes first. `schema_version = 1` follows it.
This is the software-layer schema. The title is the merge subject of pull
request 1585. `overlap.md` has one row per shared module. The SciPy-bundle
row names both pull requests:

```bash
grep -F '| `SciPy-bundle/2026.05-gfbf-2026.1` |' /tmp/sbom-demo/pr/out/overlap.md
```

```text
| `SciPy-bundle/2026.05-gfbf-2026.1` | [#1585](https://github.com/EESSI/software-layer/pull/1585), [#1728](https://github.com/EESSI/software-layer/pull/1728) |
```

`--merge-order` writes `merge-order.toml`. The extract below drops the
non-empty `builds` and `modules` arrays. The reason on position 1 is the
tool's own count.

```bash
eb-stack pr-overlap \
  --pr tests/pr_overlap_layer/prs.json \
  --easyconfigs tests/pr_overlap_layer \
  --installed tests/pr_overlap_layer/installed.txt \
  --installed-label none \
  --generated-at 2026-10-24T00:00:00Z \
  --repo-url https://github.com/EESSI/software-layer \
  --eessi-version 2026.06 \
  --merge-order \
  --out-dir /tmp/sbom-demo/pr/order
```

```text
prs=2 records=2 shared_modules=91 skipped_easyconfigs=0 out=/tmp/sbom-demo/pr/order
```

```bash
python3 - << 'PY'
from pathlib import Path
for line in Path("/tmp/sbom-demo/pr/order/merge-order.toml").read_text().splitlines():
    if line.startswith(("builds = [", "modules = [")) and "[]" not in line:
        continue
    print(line)
PY
```

```text
# Generated by `eb-stack pr-overlap`. Data only: the branch holding this file is
# regenerated on every run and must never be merged.

schema_version = 1
generated_at = "2026-10-24T00:00:00Z"
installed_source = "none"
merged = []
cycles = []
conflicts = []

[[steps]]
position = 1
pr = 1585
after = []
reason = "smallest residual build set (91)"

[[steps.saves]]
pr = 1728

[[steps]]
position = 2
pr = 1728
after = [1585]
saves = []
reason = "smallest residual build set (18)"
```

Position 1 is pull request 1585. Its `builds` array has 91 modules and
`after` is empty. Position 2 is pull request 1728. Its `builds` array has
18 modules and `after` is 1585. The same order run is what
[the how-to](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/../howto/pr-overlap.html.md) quotes.

The easyconfigs kind does not need an installed list. The recorded open
pull requests are `tests/pr_overlap_easyconfigs_open`, closed against the
same develop commit on 2026-10-24. An easyconfigs record uses
`schema_version = 2`, still after the generated-file header.

```bash
eb-stack pr-overlap --kind easyconfigs \
  --pr tests/pr_overlap_easyconfigs_open/prs.json \
  --easyconfigs tests/pr_overlap_easyconfigs_open/tree \
  --generated-at 2026-10-24T00:00:00Z \
  --repo-url https://github.com/easybuilders/easybuild-easyconfigs \
  --out-dir /tmp/sbom-demo/ec/out
```

```text
prs=4 records=4 shared_modules=1 skipped_easyconfigs=0 out=/tmp/sbom-demo/ec/out
```

```bash
sed -n '1,6p' /tmp/sbom-demo/ec/out/prs/22823.toml
```

```text

# regenerated on every run and must never be merged.

pr = 22823
head_sha = "251770fd6523b4d91847b9870d452f372217c9e7"
```

# An in-place patch

A patch can keep the easyconfig filename and the version. The rebuild
class of an installed module still changes. `rebuild-set` closes the
deployed easystacks and walks backward. The recorded inputs are the 90
easyconfigs named by `eessi-2026.06-eb-5.4.0-2026.1.yml` in the software
layer, copied from the same develop commit, with `git-2.52.0-GCCcore-15.2.0.eb`
as the changed file and `git/2.52.0-GCCcore-15.2.0` as the installed module.

```bash
eb-stack rebuild-set \
  --easyconfigs tests/sbom_recorded/rebuild \
  --installed tests/sbom_recorded/rebuild/installed.txt \
  --installed-label none \
  --generated-at 2026-10-24T00:00:00Z \
  --changed tests/sbom_recorded/rebuild/changed.txt \
  --easystack tests/sbom_recorded/rebuild/easystacks/eessi-2026.06-eb-5.4.0-2026.1.yml \
  --out-dir /tmp/sbom-demo/rebuild
```

```text
changed=1 rows=1 must-rebuild=1 review=0 no-rebuild=0 missing=0 easystacks=1 skipped_easyconfigs=0 out=/tmp/sbom-demo/rebuild
```

```bash
python3 - << 'PY'
from pathlib import Path
text = Path("/tmp/sbom-demo/rebuild/rebuild-set.md").read_text()
for line in text.splitlines():
    if line.startswith("Classes follow"):
        print(line.split(". ", 1)[0] + ".")
    if line.startswith("`--check-static` was not used"):
        print(line.split(". ", 1)[0] + ".")
PY
```

```text
Classes follow the easyconfig graph only.
`--check-static` was not used.
```

```bash
sed -n '27,29p' /tmp/sbom-demo/rebuild/rebuild-set.md
```

```text
| Changed easyconfig | Dependent | Edge kind | Class | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `git-2.52.0-GCCcore-15.2.0.eb` | `git/2.52.0-GCCcore-15.2.0` | changed | must-rebuild | patched easyconfig |
```

The report has one row: the changed git easyconfig, class must-rebuild.
The easystack entries do not depend on that git module, so the walk does
not add a second row. The report also notes each `from-commit` pin whose
tree was not passed and says the release tree was used for that pin.
`--check-static` was not passed, and the report says so. Classes follow
the easyconfig graph only.

# A component named by a CVE

The CVE names a component and a version. `component-reach` lists every
recipe in one toolchain generation that carries that component, then feeds
the recipes that contain the bytes into the same rebuild closure. The
recorded tree is `tests/component_reach_recorded`: `cURL-8.17.0-GCCcore-15.2.0.eb`
and `git-2.52.0-GCCcore-15.2.0.eb` from the same develop commit. The name
match ignores letter case and requires a whole token, so `curl` selects
the recipe named `cURL`.

```bash
eb-stack component-reach \
  --component curl \
  --version '>=8,<9' \
  --generation 2026.1 \
  --easyconfigs tests/component_reach_recorded \
  --generated-at 2026-10-24T00:00:00Z \
  --out-dir /tmp/sbom-demo/component-curl
```

```text
component=curl version=>=8,<9 generation=2026.1 carriers=2 changed=1 must-rebuild=1 review=0 no-rebuild=1 out=/tmp/sbom-demo/component-curl
```

```bash
sed -n '5,16p' /tmp/sbom-demo/component-curl/component-reach.md
```

```text
2 carriers. Closure: 1 must-rebuild, 0 review, 1 no-rebuild.

| Easyconfig | Module | Role | Version | Installed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `cURL-8.17.0-GCCcore-15.2.0.eb` | `cURL/8.17.0-GCCcore-15.2.0` | module | 8.17.0 | - |
| `git-2.52.0-GCCcore-15.2.0.eb` | `git/2.52.0-GCCcore-15.2.0` | dependency | 8.17.0 | - |

| Changed easyconfig | Dependent | Edge kind | Class | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `cURL-8.17.0-GCCcore-15.2.0.eb` | `cURL/8.17.0-GCCcore-15.2.0` | changed | must-rebuild | patched easyconfig |
| `cURL-8.17.0-GCCcore-15.2.0.eb` | `git/2.52.0-GCCcore-15.2.0` | runtime | no-rebuild | runtime dependency; links the patched package as a shared library |
```

`carriers=2` is the cURL module and git as a dependency on cURL 8.17.0.
The closure rebuilds cURL and classifies git as no-rebuild. That slice has
no `libcurl` recipe and no `curl-config` recipe.

# An easyblock or a framework class

An easyblock change reaches the recipes that name that class, a subclass,
or the implied `EB_<Name>` class. `--reverse` then lists modules that
depend on a hit and are not themselves hits. The recorded files are from
the v5.4.1 tags. `easybuild/framework/easyblock.py` defines `EasyBlock`.
`configuremake.py` defines `ConfigureMake(EasyBlock)`.
`cmakemake.py` defines `CMakeMake(ConfigureMake)`. `g/gromacs.py` defines
`EB_GROMACS(CMakeMake)`. The easyconfigs are `zfp-1.0.1-GCCcore-15.2.0.eb`
(`easyblock = 'CMakeMake'`), `make-4.4.1-GCCcore-15.2.0.eb`
(`ConfigureMake`), `GROMACS-2024.4-foss-2024a.eb` (no `easyblock` line),
and `ADIOS2-2.10.2-foss-2025b.eb` (`CMakeMake`, and it depends on
`('zfp', '1.0.1')`). The installed list names `zfp/1.0.1-GCCcore-15.2.0`.

```bash
eb-stack easyblock-reach \
  --easyblocks tests/sbom_recorded/easyblock/easyblocks \
  --framework tests/sbom_recorded/easyblock/framework \
  --easyconfigs tests/sbom_recorded/easyblock/easyconfigs \
  --file tests/sbom_recorded/easyblock/easyblocks/easybuild/easyblocks/generic/cmakemake.py \
  --installed tests/sbom_recorded/easyblock/installed.txt \
  --reverse \
  --generated-at 2026-10-24T00:00:00Z \
  --out-dir /tmp/sbom-demo/ebreach/cmake
```

```text
easyconfigs=3 installed=1 classes=2 reverse=0 out=/tmp/sbom-demo/ebreach/cmake
```

```bash
sed -n '12,26p' /tmp/sbom-demo/ebreach/cmake/reach.md
```

```text
Changed: CMakeMake, EB_GROMACS.

Reached: CMakeMake, EB_GROMACS.

## Easyconfigs

| Module | Class | Via | Detail | Installed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ADIOS2/2.10.2-foss-2025b` | `CMakeMake` | easyblock |  | no |
| `GROMACS/2024.4-foss-2024a` | `EB_GROMACS` | implied |  | no |
| `zfp/1.0.1-GCCcore-15.2.0` | `CMakeMake` | easyblock |  | yes |

## Rebuild

None.
```

Changing `cmakemake.py` reaches `CMakeMake` and `EB_GROMACS`. The three
easyconfigs are ADIOS2, GROMACS, and zfp. `make` is absent, because
`ConfigureMake` was not the change. `reverse=0`: ADIOS2 depends on zfp and
is itself a `CMakeMake` hit, so it is already in the easyconfig table.
The rebuild section is empty.

```bash
eb-stack easyblock-reach \
  --easyblocks tests/sbom_recorded/easyblock/easyblocks \
  --framework tests/sbom_recorded/easyblock/framework \
  --easyconfigs tests/sbom_recorded/easyblock/easyconfigs \
  --file tests/sbom_recorded/easyblock/framework/easybuild/framework/easyblock.py \
  --installed tests/sbom_recorded/easyblock/installed.txt \
  --reverse \
  --generated-at 2026-10-24T00:00:00Z \
  --out-dir /tmp/sbom-demo/ebreach/framework
```

```text
easyconfigs=4 installed=1 classes=5 reverse=0 out=/tmp/sbom-demo/ebreach/framework
```

```bash
sed -n '12,27p' /tmp/sbom-demo/ebreach/framework/reach.md
```

```text
Changed: ConfigureMake, EasyBlock, StopException.

Reached: CMakeMake, ConfigureMake, EB_GROMACS, EasyBlock, StopException.

## Easyconfigs

| Module | Class | Via | Detail | Installed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ADIOS2/2.10.2-foss-2025b` | `CMakeMake` | easyblock |  | no |
| `GROMACS/2024.4-foss-2024a` | `EB_GROMACS` | implied |  | no |
| `make/4.4.1-GCCcore-15.2.0` | `ConfigureMake` | easyblock |  | no |
| `zfp/1.0.1-GCCcore-15.2.0` | `CMakeMake` | easyblock |  | yes |

## Rebuild

None.
```

Changing `easybuild/framework/easyblock.py` reaches `EasyBlock`,
`StopException`, and the subclasses in the recorded easyblocks tree:
`ConfigureMake`, `CMakeMake`, and `EB_GROMACS`. `make` is now in the
table. `reverse=0` again, for the same reason as the CMakeMake run.

# The same document over MCP

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) catalog has 38 tools. `tools/list` prints
their names:

```bash
printf '%s\n' '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list","params":{}}' \
  | eb-stack mcp \
  | jq -r '.result.tools[].name'
```

```text
eb_package_inspect
eb_package_plan
eb_package_bump
eb_recipe_read
eb_recipe_list
eb_recipe_edit
eb_recipe_apply_suggestion
eb_recipe_diff
eb_recipe_write
eb_recipe_grep
eb_recipe_easyblock
eb_recipe_templates
eb_recipe_hierarchy
eb_recipe_check
eb_recipe_lint
eb_dep_versions
eb_recipe_format
eb_module_lint
eb_easyblock_dry_run
eb_build_log
eb_build_test
eb_stack_solve
eb_stack_sbom
eb_stack_order
eb_stack_easystack
eb_stack_sections
eb_stack_from_commit
eb_component_reach
eb_target_list
eb_target_doctor
eb_campaign_run
eb_campaign_status
eb_campaign_finding_claim
eb_campaign_finding_resolve
eb_pr_overlap
eb_rebuild_set
eb_easyblock_reach
eb_repro_summary
```

That is 38 tools. `eb_stack_sbom` writes the CycloneDX file `stack sbom`
writes. Its `tools/list` description reads: "Emit CycloneDX from an existing
stack lock, reading dependency edges and source checksums from the
easyconfigs the lock names." `eb_stack_sbom` reads the Cbc lock:

```bash
printf '%s\n' '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"eb_stack_sbom","arguments":{"lock":"/tmp/sbom-demo/stack.lock.json","out":"/tmp/sbom-demo/mcp-stack.cdx.json"}}}' \
  | eb-stack mcp
```

```text
{"id":2,"jsonrpc":"2.0","result":{"content":[{"text":"{\n  \"components\": 58,\n  \"lock\": \"/tmp/sbom-demo/stack.lock.json\",\n  \"out\": \"/tmp/sbom-demo/mcp-stack.cdx.json\",\n  \"recipes_read\": 58,\n  \"recipes_unreadable\": 0,\n  \"with_artifact_facts\": 55\n}","type":"text"}],"isError":false,"structuredContent":{"components":58,"lock":"/tmp/sbom-demo/stack.lock.json","out":"/tmp/sbom-demo/mcp-stack.cdx.json","recipes_read":58,"recipes_unreadable":0,"with_artifact_facts":55}}}
```

```bash
jq -S 'del(.serialNumber)' /tmp/sbom-demo/mcp-stack.cdx.json > /tmp/sbom-demo/mcp.norm.json
cmp -s /tmp/sbom-demo/lock.norm.json /tmp/sbom-demo/mcp.norm.json && echo identical
```

```text
identical
```

The MCP document matches `stack sbom` once the serial number is removed.
`components` is 58 and `with_artifact_facts` is 55, the same counts as the
lock command above. The `dependsOn` edges are the edges that command wrote
for Cbc 2.10.12.

# Contributing

This page mirrors the repository `CONTRIBUTING.md` for the documentation
site. The source of truth for development gates is the markdown file at the
repo root; keep them aligned when you change either.

# Development environment

Rust 1.88 is the minimum supported toolchain; current stable runs the main test
and lint gates. Documentation uses [pixi](https://pixi.sh):

```bash
cargo test --locked --lib
cargo test --locked --test reproduce_real_prs --test bump_emit
pixi run -e docs docbld
```

# Code style and gates

- `cargo fmt --check`
- `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` when you touch Rust
- Tests relevant to your change must pass
- New public CLI surface needs a flag entry in [CLI reference](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/reference/cli.html.md)
  and a unit or integration test under `tests/`
- Known maintainer-bump regressions in `tests/reproduce_real_prs.rs` must
  stay green (library **and** CLI auto-bump)

# Documentation

Primary docs live in orgmode under `docs/orgmode/` (Diataxis). Edit there,
then build. The Sphinx site includes an in-tree Rust API (`crates/eb_stack/`)
via `sphinx-rustdocgen` + `sphinxcontrib_rust` (same path as rsx-rs).

```bash
# once: isolated system-Python environment for the native Rust extension
python3 -m venv .venv-docs
export RUSTFLAGS='-C linker=cc'
export CARGO_TARGET_X86_64_UNKNOWN_LINUX_GNU_LINKER=cc
.venv-docs/bin/pip install 'sphinx>=9,<10' shibuya sphinx-sitemap \
  sphinx-copybutton sphinx-design 'sphinxcontrib-rust>=1,<2' \
  'sphinx-rustdoc-postprocess>=0.1,<0.2'
cargo install sphinx-rustdocgen

export EB_STACK_DOCS_PYTHON=$PWD/.venv-docs/bin/python
pixi run -e docs docbld
scripts/check-doc-links.sh docs/build
pixi run -e docs linkcheck
# HTML -> docs/build/index.html
```

The Sphinx task treats warnings as errors. The rendered-link check rejects
links to generated RST and incorrect source-edit targets; the Lychee task
checks the rendered site and README links.

`sphinxcontrib-rust` contains a native Rust extension. The explicit linker
environment keeps that extension on the host Rust/C linker rather than a
linker injected by the documentation package environment.

Do not hand-edit generated `docs/source/**/*.rst` or `docs/source/crates/`.

# Packaging campaigns

Follow `AGENTS.md`, `skills/annual-bump/SKILL.md` (generation rebuild), and
`skills/new-package/SKILL.md` (conda-forge/Spack: new recipe). Run
`skills/verify-recipe/SKILL.md` over what they emit before a build or a push,
and `skills/tool-repair/SKILL.md` when the emitted file needed a hand
correction: a manual fix that does not return as a regression test is a
defect this tool reproduces on the next run. Keep site hostnames, paths,
credentials, scheduler sizing, and private module names in the site target
layer. Public files contain reusable package intent and target topology.

# Releasing

Version source of truth is `version` in root `Cargo.toml`. Keep these aligned:

1. `Cargo.toml` / `pixi.toml` `version`
2. `CITATION.cff` `version` and `date-released` for a published version
3. `docs/source/conf.py` `release`
4. `CHANGELOG.md` version heading and release date

Tag `vX.Y.Z` and push the tag. The release workflow builds the Linux archive
and checksum and publishes the GitHub Release.

# Changelog

The tagged release is 0.3.0. Cargo, CITATION, and Sphinx still report
**0.3.0**. Changes since that tag are the Unreleased section of
[CHANGELOG.md](https://github.com/HaoZeke/eb-stack/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).

The version-one design provides:

- one canonical package plan for conda-forge, Spack, and EasyBuild;
- planned CycloneDX plus per-profile Resolvo locks;
- one conventional EasyBuild recipe per installable profile;
- package-source catalogs, source-root discovery, and recursive closure;
- in-solver stack pin fallback and candidate exclusions;
- layered target routing and persisted typed build campaigns;
- independent resolves, builds, and binary-verified claims;
- matching CLI, Model Context Protocol (MCP), new-package skill, and
  annual-bump skill workflows, with recipe lint and the stack software
  bill of materials (SBOM) among the MCP tools;
- graph ordering, easystack emission, and Jenkins section regrouping;
- a reproduction scoreboard summary;
- easyblock dry-run, module lint, and build tools on the MCP server.

The scaffold/compatibility command surface is removed rather than maintained
alongside the canonical workflow.
